Cryoglobulins

Q. What are cryoglobulins?

●      Proteins that precipitate at temperatures below 37 degrees and re-solubilize when blood is warmed again to 37 degrees.

   

Q. What are the two primary mechanisms by which cryoglobulins cause symptoms?

·       Hyperviscosity

·       Immune complex deposition → leading to complement fixation and vasculitis.

 

 

Q. What are common clinical findings in cryoglobulinemia?

·       Peripheral neuropathy

·       MSK findings (arthralgia is common)

·       Dermatologic manifestations (ulcers, necrosis, purpuric macules, and papules etc)

·       Renal manifestations (AKI, glomerulonephritis)

 

Q. What is the Meltzer triad?

1.     Purpura

2.     Arthralgia

3.     Fatigue/weakness (“asthenia”)

 

Q. How does measurement of serum viscosity help predict severity in cryoglobulinemia?

·       cp values correlate with likelihood of clinical manifestations

·       Values greater than 4.0 cp are typically associated with clinical symptoms

·       Symptoms are less likely with less than 3.0 cp

 

Q. What percent of normal individuals have cryoglobulins?

 

- Approximately 40 % of normal individuals may have small quantities of cryoglobulins detectable.

 

Q. What are the 3 underlying causes of cryoglobulins?

 

●      They typically have either an underlying

○      Inflammatory

○      Infectious

○      Malignant process

 

Q. How common are cryoglobulins in HIV, Hep B and connective tissue diseases?

 

- All around 15%.

 

Q. What percent of Hep C patients have cryoglobulins?

 

- Approximately 50% of all patients infected with HCV have cryoglobulinemia but only a minority are symptomatic.

 

Q. How are cryoglobulins classified - what is the name of the classification system?

 

- The Brouet classification based on their immunoglobulin clonality.

 

Table: Cryoglobulin Classification https://doi.org/10.1002/ajh.22023

Cryoglobulin Type

%

Components

Disease Association

Type I (simple)

10-15

Monoclonal immunoglobulins (IgG, IgM, or IgA) or Bence Jones protein/monoclonal free light chains

Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, multiple myeloma, monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), light chain disease

Type II (mixed)

50-60

Monoclonal immunoglobulin (IgM, IgG, or IgA) and polyclonal immunoglobulin (mostly IgG)

Hepatitis C, essential cryoglobulinemia, Sjögren's syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic lymphocytic leukemia

Type III (mixed)

30-40

Polyclonal immunoglobulins of all isotypes

Sjögren's syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, viral infections (e.g., Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, CMV, EBV, HIV), endocarditis, bacterial infections, biliary cirrhosis

 

Q. What is a type I cryoglobulinemia?

 

●      Monoclonal immunoglobulin, typically IgG or IgM, and less commonly IgA or free Ig light chains.

●      Typically associated with B-cell LPD such as LPL or MM.

 

Q. Describe type II cryoglobulinemia?

 

●      Type II cryoglobulinemia consists of a mixture of polyclonal IgG with a monoclonal IgM directed against the polyclonal IgG (ie rheumatoid factor RF). Aka “mixed type”

●      This is the most common type → associated with viral infection

●      Hep C in >80% of cases

●      Can also be seen with Hep B and HIV.

 

Q. Describe type III cryoglobulinemia?

●      Type III cryoglobulinemia consists of a polyclonal IgG with a polyclonal IgM RF directed against the polyclonal IgG.

●      Typically seen in patients with autoimmune disorders such as SLE or Sjogren's.

 

Q. How do you detect cryoglobulins?

●      Collect a warm specimen (don’t allow to cool)

●      Allow to clot at 37 degrees (so cryoglobulins don’t precipitate yet)

●      Separate the serum and then → refrigerate serum at 4 degrees

●      Typically this is refrigerated for approximately 3-5 days

●      Measure precipitate

○      VGH uses these special tubes that have quantitative markings on them

○      Concentration can be determined → spectrophotometrically

○      +/- further testing such as immunofixation can be performed to characterize the cryoglobulin (type I, II or III). Dr. Pudek said immunofixation is not done routinely at VGH)

●      Ensure the precipitate can be redissolved at 37 degrees (required for definition of cryoglobulin, although Dr Pudek said this is not done routinely at VGH)

 

List 4 clinical manifestations of cryoglobulins (Type I, Type II and III)

●      Clinical manifestations associated with type I cryoglobulinemia (are related to hyperviscosity and thrombosis):

○      Acrocyanosis

○      Retinal hemorrhage

○      Severe Raynaud phenomenon with digital ulceration

○      Livedo reticularis

○      Purpura

○      Arterial thrombosis

●      Clinical manifestations associated with types II and III cryoglobulinemia:

○      Joint involvement (usually, arthralgias in the proximal interphalangeal [PIP] joints, metacarpophalangeal [MCP] joints, knees, and ankles)

○      Fatigue

○      Myalgias

○      Renal immune-complex disease

○      Cutaneous vasculitis

○      Peripheral neuropathy

 

What is the Meltzer triad?

●      Triad seen in up to 25-30% of Type II and Type III cryoglobulinemia:

○      Purpura

○      Arthralgia

○      Fatigue/Weakness

 

What are the diseases associated with the three types of cryoglobulinemia?

●      Type I is observed in lymphoproliferative disorders (eg, MGUS, multiple myeloma, Waldenström macroglobulinemia, CLL).

●      Types II and III are observed in chronic inflammatory diseases such as chronic liver disease, infections (chronic HCV infection), and coexistent connective-tissue diseases (SLE, Sjögren syndrome). Mixed cryoglobulinemia (type 2) is rarely associated with lymphoproliferative disorders.

 

What are the infections associated with cryoglobulinemia?

·       Viral

·       Hepatitis A, B, and C

·       HIV, EBV, CMV, adenovirus; chikungunya

·       Bacterial

·       Endocarditis, streptococcal infections

·       syphilis, Lyme disease, leprosy, Q fever, brucellosis

·       Fungal – Coccidioidomycosis

·       Parasitic - Malaria, toxoplasmosis, others

What are other disorders associated with cryoglobulinemia?

·       Autoimmune diseases - SLE, RA, Sjögren syndrome

·       Vasculitis-Polyarteritis nodosa (especially hepatitis B–associated), Henoch-Schönlein purpura

·       Lymphoproliferative disorders - Waldenström macroglobulinemia, multiple myeloma, lymphoma, leukemia (eg, CLL, HCL)

·       Renal diseases -Proliferative glomerulonephritis

·       Liver diseases - Hepatitis A, B, and C (30-98% of patients with HCV infection have cryoglobulins, especially type II);cirrhosis

Autoimmune Lymphoproliferative Syndrome (ALPS)

 

What is ALPS?

●      Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome

●      Defective Lymphocyte apoptosis

●      Chronic non-malignant proliferation of polyclonal lymphocytes

●      LAD & HSM

●      Develop autoimmune disease, increased risk of lymphoma

●      Autoimmune cytopenias

 

What is the mutated gene in ALPS (3)?

●      FAS

○      Mostly AD

●      FASLG (FAS-ligand)

○      Some AD, mostly AR

●      CASP10 (Caspase 10)

○      AD

FAST TRACK ALPS

·       FAS: primary gene involved (FAS/CD95 mutation).

·       T: T-cell abnormalities (defective apoptosis of lymphocytes).

·       R: Regulators fail, leading to lymphoproliferation and autoimmunity.

·       A: Autoimmunity, especially autoimmune cytopenias.

·       CK: Chronic apoptosis defects due to mutation in key apoptotic pathway genes.

·       ALPS: Autoimmune LymphoProliferative Syndrome.

KEY GENES IN ALPS

“F-CAN”:

·        F: FAS

·        C: CASP10

·        A: Apoptosis-related mutations (FASLG)

·        N: NRAS/KRAS

 

Q. What are the clinical manifestations of ALPS?

 

-        Patients with ALPS have a defect in the → lymphocyte apoptotic pathway

-        Defective lymphocyte apoptosis leads to → chronic non-malignant lymphoproliferation, autoimmune disease, and increased risk of secondary cancers (eg lymphoma).

-        Typically have enlarged lymph nodes, and spleen, and autoimmune cytopenias.

 

Q. What are the diagnostic criteria for ALPS?

 

Required:

-        1. Chronic (> 6 months), nonmalignant, noninfectious lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly or both

-        2. Elevated CD3+, TCRαβ+, CD4−, CD8− DNT cells (≥ 1.5% of total lymphocytes or 2.5% of CD3+ lymphocytes) in the setting of normal or elevated lymphocyte counts

Accessory

 

Primary

-        1. Defective lymphocyte apoptosis (in 2 separate assays)

-        2. Somatic or germline pathogenic mutation in FAS, FASLG, or CASP10

Secondary

-        1. Elevated plasma sFASL levels (>200 pg/mL) OR elevated plasma interleukin-10 levels (>20 pg/mL) OR elevated serum or plasma vitamin B12 levels (> 1500 ng/L) OR elevated plasma interleukin -18 levels > 500 pg/mL

-        2. Typical immunohistological findings as reviewed by an experienced hematopathologist

-        3. Autoimmune cytopenias (hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, or neutropenia) AND elevated immunoglobulin G levels (polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia)

-        4. Family history of a nonmalignant/noninfectious lymphoproliferation with or without autoimmunity

A definitive diagnosis is based on → the presence of both required criteria plus one primary accessory criterion.

A probable diagnosis is based on → the presence of both required criteria plus one secondary accessory criterion. (Blood. 2010 Oct 7; 116(14): e35–e40.)

 

Q. What are the 3 most common mutations in ALPS?

·       Mutations in FAS or FASL gene of caspase 10

 

Q. What is the immunophenotype of ALPS?

·       CD3+, 4/8- (DNT, all ALPS subtypes have increased DNT cells), TCRαβ+, CD45RA+ (naive T cells), CD45RO-, T-cell population in the PB and BM.

·       May be 57+ but are 25- (CD25 is a marker for T regulatory cells, ALPS has decreased CD4+ and CD25+ regulatory T cells)


 


When does ALPS present?

●      Median age of 3

 

What is the relationship between ALPS and Lymphoma?

●      Increased risk of lymphoma

○      15-50x

○      FAS is a tumour suppressor gene

●      15% Lymphoma by age 30

 

What is the treatment for ALPS?

●      IST: immunosuppressive therapy

●      Splenectomy → if symptomatic or if ruptures

Subtype

Severely reduced serum immunoglobulins (Igs) with profoundly decreased or absent B cells (Agammaglobulinemia)

• Recurrent sinopulmonary infections.

• AID/UNG defects impair class switching.
• CD40/CD40L cause lack of germinal centers.

Isotype/light chain deficiencies with normal B cells

• SIgAD may occur alone or with IgG subclass deficiency.

Specific Antibody Deficiency (SAD)

• Failure to produce sufficient antibodies to specific microbes.

• Sinopulmonary infections.

Transient Hypogammaglobulinemia of Infancy (THI)

• Resolves by age 5.

CID combined immunodeficiency

 

What does the term "primary immunodeficiency" refer to?

 

●      The term "primary immunodeficiency" denotes diseases resulting from inherited defects of the immune system.

●      Many distinct disorders have been described

 

What are the “combined immunodeficiency (CID) syndromes”?

●      A heterogeneous group of immunodeficiency disorders arising from a disturbance in the development and function of both T and B cells (cellular and humoral immunity) and may also involve natural killer (NK) cells.

●      Caused by mutations in genes crucial for T and B cell (+/-NK cell) development

○      May only affect T cells, but the B cells won’t have an effective humoral immunity without normal T cell signaling

○      Previously classified according to their affected cells (T-B+NK+, T-B+NK-, T-B-NK+, or T-B-NK-), but now classified based on mutation

Q. Name 5 combined immunodeficiency syndromes that are NOT “severe”

1.     Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome

2.     WHIM Syndrome (Warts, hypogammaglobulinemia, infections, and myelokathexis) syndrome

3.     DiGeorge syndrome

4.     Ataxia-telangiectasia

5.     Nijmegen breakage syndrome

6.     Omenn syndrome

7.     Cartilage-hair hypoplasia/short-limbed dwarfism

8.     Purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency (“Adenosine deaminase deficiency”)

9.     CD40 and CD40 ligand deficiencies (“Hyperimmunoglobulin M syndromes")

 

Disorder

Gene

Pathogenesis

Clinical features

WAS

Defective actin cytoskeleton reorganization due to mutations in the WAS protein (WASP).

Thrombocytopenia, small platelets, eczema, autoimmune disease, bacterial infections

Ataxia-telangiectasia

Mutation in the ATM gene leads to defective DNA repair and increased sensitivity to ionizing radiation.  

Ataxia, telangiectasias, increased AFP, increased sensitivity to ionizing radiation

Developmental defect in the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches due to deletion on chromosome 22.

Congenital heart disease, facial dysmorphism, immunodeficiency, ADHD

Nijmegen breakage syndrome

Defective DNA repair pathways due to NBS1 (nibrin) gene mutation, causing chromosomal instability. 

Microcephaly, progressive mental retardation, sensitivity to ionizing radiation, predisposition to cancer

Omenn syndrome

 

RAG 1 & 2

(remember the middle east Omen people use Rugs(RAG1/2) to welcome the guest but the guest against the host)

T cells are auto-reactive and cause the GVHD phenotype.

Chronic erythematous skin inflammation (early onset erythroderma). Eosinophilia, failure to thrive, LAD, HSM, diarrhea, low Ig levels (except IgE, which is elevated), low T cell levels, and no B cells

WHIM syndrome

Warts, hypogammaglobulinemia, immunodeficiency, and myelokathexis.

SCID severe combined immunodeficiency

What is “severe” combined immunodeficiency (SCID)?

●      Combined immunodeficiencies are termed "severe" → when they lead to early death from overwhelming infection → typically in the first year of life.

●      SCID can be categorized as typical SCID or, if less severe, leaky SCID based upon the severity of T cell qualitative and quantitative deficiency.

●      CID is milder → no early death in 1st year of life

Q. What are the typical clinical findings of SCID?

●      Recurrent infections (severe) → recurrent fevers in a child

○      Persistent mucocutaneous candidiasis (thrush), mouth ulcers

○      CMV, EBV, Rotavirus, norovirus, RSV, VZV, HSV, measles, influenza, parainfluenza (commonly fatal)

○      Opportunistic infections

■      PJP

○      Live attenuated virus vaccines cause severe/fatal infection

●      Chronic diarrhea

●      Failure to thrive

●      Unexplained lymphopenia

●      Absent Lymphoid tissue

○      Absence of thymic shadow

○      Thymus is generally small and devoid of lymphocytes

●      Increased resting energy expenditure (hypermetabolism)

●      Note: May not have Sx for first 6 months due to humoral immunity provided by mom

●      Patients may also suffer from graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) prior to definitive treatment due to:

○      Transfusion of blood products containing viable lymphocytes, which can lead to rapidly fatal GVHD

○      Transplacental passage of alloreactive maternal T cells

●      A family history of SCID (seen in <20 percent of cases)

Q. What are the typical Lab findings of SCID?

●      Generally low absolute lymphocyte count

○      Abnormalities of lymphocyte subpopulations as determined by flow cytometry

○      Low/absent autologous CD3+ T cells <300 cells/uL:

■      <300 cells/microL in typical SCID

■      >300 to <1500 cells/microL in leaky SCID

○      The T cell count may be normal or high in some cases due to:

■      Presence of maternal T cells in the peripheral circulation or

■      Abnormal expansion of a few clones (eg, Omenn syndrome).

○      B/NK cells may be reduced

●      Absent/low T cell proliferation to mitogens (Phytohemagglutinin PHA)

●      Hypogammaglobulinemia

○      May be obscured by maternal IgG in infancy

■      IgM and IgA will be LOW!

Q. What are the treatment options for SCID?

-        Stem cell transplant = definitive treatment

-        Fatal within 1st year of life without

-        Treatment prior to SCT

-        Protective isolation

-        Avoidance of live vaccine

-        Irradiated, leukoreduced blood products

-        Antibody replacement (IVIG)

-        Prophylaxis with PJP, fungal, Herpes, RSV

 

Q. What are 6 common Gene Mutations in SCID?

Try to remember 6

T-, B+

-        JAK3, CD3-delta, epsilon and zeta chains, IL2Ra chain (CD25)

T-, B-

-        RAG 1, RAG2 and ADA

 

What are the diagnostic criteria for severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)?

Definitive diagnosis

Patient less than 2 years of age with either:

an absolute CD3 T cell count of less than 300/mm3, or

an absolute CD3 T cell count of greater than 300/mm3 with absent naïve CD3/CD45RA T cells, and at least 1 of the following:

 

Male with deleterious mutation in the X-linked IL2RG gene encoding the cytokine receptor common gamma chain (gamma-c).

 

Male or female patient with deleterious homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in any of the genes listed in the Gene Defects table other than IL2RG.

 

ADA activity of less than 2% of control or mutations in both alleles of the ADA gene.

 

Engraftment of transplacentally acquired maternal T cells.

Probable diagnosis

 

Male or female patient less than 2 years of age with:

 

(a) less than 20% CD3+ T cells, an absolute lymphocyte count of less than 3000/mm3, and proliferative responses to mitogens less than 10% of control or

(b) the presence of maternal lymphocytes in the circulation.

 

Name 2 other combined immunodeficiency syndromes with a similar clinical presentation to SCID that are characterized by thymic agenesis or partial T cell deficiency and opportunistic infections

 

●      1) DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome - thymic hypoplasia, hypocalcaemia, outflow tract defects of the heart, and dysmorphic facies, part of CATCH 22: Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, and Hypocalcaemia

●      2) CHARGE syndrome - coloboma, heart defects, atresia choanae (also known as choanal atresia), growth retardation, genital abnormalities, and ear abnormalities

●      Both have thymic agenesis or partial T cell deficiency.

●      They are the most commonly seen genetic syndromes detected by newborn screening that can mimic SCID

●      Genetic testing to rule out these diagnoses should be completed prior to HCT since thymic agenesis will not improve without thymic transplant.

●      Ataxia telangiectasia is another one easy to remember (Molecular Insights Into the Causes of Human Thymic Hypoplasia With Animal Models - PMC)

CVID common variable immunodeficiency

 

What is CVID?

 

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) → heterogeneous group with failed B-cell maturation, impaired antibody production, reduced serum immunoglobulins

 

CVID is defined by:

·       Low total serum concentrations of immunoglobulin G (IgG), as well as low immunoglobulin A (IgA) and/or immunoglobulin M (IgM)

·       Poor or absent response to immunization

·       Characteristic clinical manifestations in the absence of any other detectable molecular defect (such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia [XLA] or hyperimmunoglobulin M [HIGM] syndrome (HIGM is combined b- and t- cell disorder) and others)

 

1. Definition and Diagnosis

·        CVID is a primary immunodeficiency characterized by:

o            Low levels of serum IgG, IgA, and/or IgM.

o            Reduced or absent specific antibody production.

o            Serum IgG is typically < 400 mg/dL.

·        Diagnosis:

o            Most commonly diagnosed in adults aged 20-40 years, but can occur in children and older adults.

o            Diagnosis in children under 4 is delayed due to physiological immaturity mimicking CVID.

o            Average delay in diagnosis is 6-7 years, with symptoms often present for years before diagnosis.

2. Clinical Manifestations

·        Infections:

o            Recurrent sinopulmonary infections (pneumonia, bronchitis, sinusitis, otitis) are the most common symptoms.

o            Infections are due to a lack of protective antibodies.

·        Inflammatory and Autoimmune Complications:

o            Two main phenotypes:

1.                                            Infections only.

2.                                            Infections + inflammatory/autoimmune complications (e.g., lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, autoimmune cytopenias, enteropathy, granulomatous disease).

o            Autoimmune diseases:

§            Most common: immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) and autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA).

§            Others: rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, thyroid disease, etc.

o            Granulomatous disease:

§            Similar to sarcoidosis, found in lungs, lymph nodes, liver, and skin.

§            Associated with increased autoimmunity.

o            Gastrointestinal disease:

§            Chronic diarrhea, malabsorption, and nodular lymphoid hyperplasia.

§            Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is common.

o            Lymphoma and malignancies:

§            Increased risk of B-cell lymphomas (especially non-Hodgkin lymphoma).

§            Other cancers (e.g., stomach cancer) may also be increased.

3. Treatment

·        Immunoglobulin (Ig) replacement therapy:

·        Management of complications:

4. Prognosis and Survival

·        Survival:

o            Improved with Ig therapy, but still lower than age-matched controls.

o            Major causes of death: Chronic lung disease, malignancies, and infections.

·        Predictors of mortality:

o            Lower baseline IgG, fewer peripheral B cells, and higher IgM at diagnosis.

5. Pathogenesis

·        Immunologic abnormalities:

o            Reduced memory B cells (especially isotype-switched memory B cells: IgD-IgM-CD27+).

o            Loss of plasma cells in bone marrow and tissues.

·        Genetic factors:

o            Mutations in genes like ICOS, CD19, TACI, and others are found in a small subset of patients.

o            TACI mutations are associated with CVID but are not diagnostic, as they can also be found in healthy individuals.

6. Monitoring and Follow-Up

·        Regular monitoring:

o            Serum IgG levels, complete blood counts, and chemistry panels.

o            Lung disease: Chest X-ray or MRI, lung function tests.

o            Gastrointestinal symptoms: Endoscopy if symptomatic.

o            Lymphadenopathy: Biopsy if persistent or suspicious.

7. Key Statistics

·        Prevalence: 1 in 25,000 to 1 in 50,000.

·        Inflammatory/autoimmune complications:

o            71% in European cohort.

o            68% in US cohort.

·        Lymphoma incidence: 8.2% in US cohort.

·        Mortality: 19.6% in US cohort over 4 decades.

Lymphocytic variant HES (L-HES)

 

What is L-HES?

●      A secondary/reactive HES caused by → cytokine producing T cell subsets identified in the peripheral blood

●      L-HES is characterized by a predominance of → skin and soft tissue involvement including LAD (although other clinical manifestations of HES, including cardiovascular, pulmonary, and rheumatological/articular involvement, are also present).

●      The prevalence of this variant among all patients with HES is not well-defined.

Are the cytokine producing T cells in L-HES clonal?

●      ? This disorder may evolve to lymphoma

 

What serum Ig is characteristically increased in patients with L-HES?

●      IgE

●      In the largest cohort of patients with CD3-CD4+ associated L-HES reported, the majority of patients had elevated serum immunoglobulin E (IgE), skin involvement, and lymphadenopathy.

 

L-HES is caused by cytokine producing T cell subsets - what is the specific cytokine they produce to cause eosinophilia?

●      IL-5 → stimulates eos

●      In addition to IL-5, the abnormal T cells produce other T helper type 2 (Th2) cytokines such as → IL-4 and IL-13, as well as GM-CSF.

●      The effects of these Th2 cytokines on other cells (eg, B cells) account for associated biologic features of L-HES → eg B cell stimulation leads to increased IgE synthesis and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia

 

What is the most frequently reported abnormal T cell phenotype in L-HES

●      CD3-CD4+ T cells

●      Other

○      CD4+7-

○      CD3+8-4- (DNT)

Do patients with L-HES typically have lymphocytosis?

●      No

●      Total lymphocyte counts were elevated in just one-third of patients

What mutation is associated with L-HES?

●      STAT3 → “signal transducer and activator of transcription 3” gene

●      Molecular disease mechanisms remain largely unknown.

●      However, one study identified a signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) gene gain-of-function mutation in → CD3-CD4+ T cells from one patient, and although the mutation was not found in two other patients, evidence for upregulation of STAT3-dependent pathways was found

●      Unclear relationship to pathogenesis at this time.

●      Note: STAT3 is also associated with T-LGL (40%), CLPD-NK (30%), ALCL, ENKTL

●      STAT5 is associated with CML, AML, ALL, and Hodgkin lymphoma.

Granuloma

 

Types of Bone Marrow Granulomas

Type

Features

Comments

Lipogranuloma

Foamy histiocytes abundant

Most common type of BM granuloma

 

Lipid-like vacuoles

Found in up to 10% of BM specimens

 

Admixed lymphocytes common

More common in old age groups

 

 

May become more epithelioid

Epithelioid granuloma

Distinct collection of histiocytes with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm

May be caseating or non-caseating

More likely to be infectious if caseating

 

May see multinucleation of histiocytes

Associated with variety of infections and noninfectious systemic illnesses including Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma

 

Admixed eosinophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, or neutrophils may be present

Rarely associated with drug treatments including Bacille Calmette Guérin (BCG)

Ring-shaped granuloma

Circular shape with central empty space; occasional cases exhibit central lipid material

Described in Q fever (Coxiella burnetii)

 

Ring of histiocytes with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm

Also seen in variety of other disorders including CMV and Lyme disease

 

Variable numbers of inflammatory cells

 

Foreign body granuloma

Epithelioid granuloma with foreign body type multinucleated cells

Very rarely encountered in BM

 

May contain polarizable foreign material

Most often linked to prior surgery in area

 

May be present in patients with familial crystal storage diseases such as oxalosis

Crystal deposition elicits foreign body response

Neoplasm-associated granulomas

Epithelioid granulomas and increased epithelioid histiocytes may be admixed with neoplastic disorders involving BM

Most common in patient with BM involvement by Hodgkin lymphoma or peripheral T-cell lymphoma

 

 

Different Types of Granulomas in Bone Marrow

Type

Features

Epithelioid granuloma without necrosis

(Non-caseating)

Aggregates of histiocytes that could be cohesive or loose and ill defined in immunocompromised patients

Epithelioid granuloma with necrosis

(Necrotizing = caseating)

Central necrosis surrounded by palisading histiocytes and occasional giant cells with numerous nuclei (Langhans-type giant cells)

Sarcoid-like epithelioid granulomas

Compact, discrete epithelioid granulomas often surrounded by small lymphocytes and occasional multinucleated giant cells, not specific for sarcoidosis

Lipid granuloma (lipogranuloma)

Most common type; up to 10% of all BMs

Aggregates of foamy histiocytes containing lipid vacuoles, often surrounded by small lymphocytes and occasional multinucleated giant cells

Ring epithelioid granuloma

Aggregates of histiocytes forming ring around lipid vacuole

Q-fever (Coxiella burnetii), CMV, Lyme disease

Foreign body-type granuloma

Uncommon in bone marrow; multinucleated giant cells containing exogenous foreign material usually present

Granulomas associated with neoplasms

Granulomas may occasionally be present in bone marrow associated with lymphomas, more common in Hodgkin than non-Hodgkin lymphomas; granulomas can also be seen in bone marrow associated with other malignant tumors, including metastatic carcinomas

Drug-induced granulomas

Isolated reports on bone marrow granulomas caused by administration of drugs, including procainamide, sulfonamide, methyl dopa, and phenytoin that may disappear following cessation of drugs

Sarcoidosis is widely known to be one of auto-immune diseases which cause several granulomas with giant multi-nuclear cells derived from macrophages. In the case of sarcoidosis, asteroid body (inclusion body in the cytoplasm) is the hallmark for the pathological diagnosis.

Chronic Granulomatous Disease

 

Approach to neutropenia:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4629920/

 

Q. What is chronic granulomatous disease?

 

- Refers to a group of disorders which result in failure of phagocytic cells to kill ingested organisms

- Typically, there is a defect in the generation of functional NADPH oxidase activity through a variety of different mutations.

- This causes a failure to generate → the respiratory burst.

Another disease associated with NADPH -> G6PD

Key Differences Between G6PD Deficiency and CGD

Feature

G6PD Deficiency

Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)

Defect

G6PD enzyme in RBCs

NADPH oxidase in phagocytes

Pathogenesis

RBCs unable to handle oxidative stress

Impaired ROS production in phagocytes

Main Symptoms

Hemolytic anemia

Recurrent bacterial and fungal infections

Triggers

Oxidative stress

Catalase-positive organisms

Affected Cells

Red blood cells (RBCs)

Neutrophils, macrophages

Treatment

Avoid triggers, manage hemolysis

Prophylactic therapy, stem cell transplant

 

What is the mutation causing CGD?

-        CGD arises from mutations that result in the loss or functional inactivation of one of the subunits of the NADPH oxidase complex

-        X-linked CGD

-        CYBB gene (Cytochrome B)

-        Autosomal

-        CYBA

-        NCF1 (Neutrophil Cytoplasmic factor)

-        NCF2

-        NCF4

What are the clinical manifestations of CGD?

-        Formation of granulomata

-        Recurrent infection:

-        Pneumonia

-        Abscesses

-        Septic Arthritis

-        Osteomyelitis

-        Bacteremia/fungemia

-        Cellulitis

-        Atypical infections

-        Catalase positive bacteria

-        Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia marcescens, Listeria species, E. coli, Klebsiella species, Pseudomonas cepacia, a.k.a. Burkholderia cepacia, Nocardia.

-        Fungi

-        Aspergillus species, Candida species

-        Other:

-        Growth retardation

-        Chronic pulmonary disease

-        Autoimmune disorders

 

Q. How can CGD be diagnosed - what are 2 tests?

●      1) Nitroblue-tetrazolium → is a test in which NBT is reduced to an insoluble blue compound called formazan by → NADPH oxidase

○      When exposed to pathogens or stimulants, healthy neutrophils produce superoxide via the NADPH oxidase enzyme complex.

○      CGD has no formation of blue formazan due to lack of NADPH oxidase

○      In CGD the no blue color is produced.

○      Replaced by DHR

 

 

●      2) Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry assay → which can measure NADPH activity

○      Whole blood stained with DHR & incubated

○      Neutrophils are stimulated with a potent activator (e.g., phorbol myristate acetate, PMA) to produce superoxide radicals

○      Superoxide radicals oxidise DHR to → Rhodamine

○      Rhodamine is fluorescent

○      Can be detected by flow cytometer

○      CGD has no/decreased conversion of DHR → Rhodamine due to lack of NADPH oxidase = decreased fluorescent signal compared to normal

 

 

 

 

What are is the differential for two populations, one with abnormal DHR flow testing?

1.     X-linked CGD Carrier

a.     Ie. female who carries CYBB gene mutation

2.     Affected patient with transplantation and <100% chimerism

a.     Donor cell population = normal

b.     Patient cell population = deficient

3.     Pre-stimulated neutrophils

a.     Neutrophils that have already been stimulated/ degranulated before the test was done will not have any fluorescence

Always need a normal “transit” control that has had the same conditions

Q. What are the genetics of CGD?

●      Mutations in CYBB gene which is X-linked and accounts for approximately 70% of CGD cases.

●      Other autosomal recessive gene mutations include → CYBA, NCF1, NCF2, and NCF4.

 

Q. What is McLeod syndrome?

·       Mutations of XK gene (located on X chromosome) → absence of Kx protein → causes decreased Kell antigen → secondary to membrane destabilization

·       Associated with increased acanthocytes

·       May be associated with X-linked Chronic granulomatous disease if gene mutation encompasses both genes on X chromosome

·       Association with neuroacanthocytosis (a group of genetic conditions that are characterized by movement disorders and acanthocytosis (abnormal, spiculated or star-shaped red blood cells)

·       Four syndromes are classified as neuroacanthocytosis:

-        Chorea-acanthocytosis

-        McLeod syndrome

-        Huntington's disease-like 2 (HDL2)

-        Panthothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN)

·       Note not the same as Swyer-James-Macleod Syndrome (SJMS), which is a rare pulmonary disorder characterized by unilateral hyperlucency of the lung.

 

Sample interpretation of results

DHR flow cytometry results show [normal/deficient/abnormal] oxidative burst activity. This suggests that patient is likely to have [no evidence of CGD/Chronic Granulomatous Disease, X-linked CGD, Autosomal Recessive CGD, Carrier State]. Additional genetic testing, including sequencing of NADPH oxidase subunits (e.g., CYBB, NCF1, CYBA), may be necessary for confirming the specific genetic mutation in suspected CGD cases. Correlation with clinical findings and other laboratory or radiologic results for a final diagnosis.

 

Tumor-like lesions

·       Reactive B-cell-rich lymphoid proliferations that can mimic lymphoma

·       IgG4-related disease

·       Unicentric Castleman disease

·       Idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease

·       KSHV/HHV8-associated multicentric Castleman disease

IgG4-related disorder

 

What is IgG4 related disease - 5 features

·       Definition - Fibroinflammatory condition with characteristic clinical, pathologic, and serologic features

1.     Fibroinflammatory condition

2.     Tumefactive (puffy) lesions

3.     Fibrosis

4.     Increased serum IgG4 ~70% cases

5.     Eosinophilia

What is the diagnostic criteria for IgG4-related disorder Diagnostic Criteria:

·       Characteristic Histology in all organs (PATHOLOGY)

○      Dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate

○      Storiform fibrosis

○      Obliterative phlebitis[QZ1] 

●      Increase IgG4 plasma cells

○      IgG4/IgG plasma cell ratio >40% used or

○      Increase in IgG4-bearing plasma cells per HPF

■      HPF is less reliable as many different tissue types have different plasma cell content.

Cautious in LN and BM!! Would prefer tissue sample itself

·        For lung: Increased number of IgG4(+) plasma cells in tissue sections [> 10 IgG4(+) plasma cells per HPF, IgG4/IgG (+) plasma cell ratio of > 40%]

·        For kidney: At least moderate increase: > 10 IgG4(+) cells/40x field in most concentrated area

o   Some cases show marked increase, > 30 IgG4(+) cells/40x field

·        For thyroid/head/neck: IgG4(+) plasma cells > 20/HPF

o   IgG4(+)/IgG(+) plasma cell ratio > 30%

·        For lymph node : Increased IgG4(+) plasma cells, usually > 50 per HPF

o            IgG4(+)/IgG(+) plasma cells > 40%

 

Note: IgG4 usually low concentration in serum <1g/L

●      In patients with AI pancreatitis, increase in IgG4 (6.63 g/L)

●      Normal range for all Gamma globulins is 6-15 g/L total

What are the 4 Common Manifestations of IgG4-RD? – pancreas, salivary, kidney, uroaroto

1.     Autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP)

2.     Glandular swelling (salivary and lacrimal glands; thyroid)

3.     Retroperitoneal fibrosis (often aorta and ureters)

4.     Tubulointerstitial fibrosis (IgG4 related tubulointerstitial nephritis)

Who gets IgG4-RD?

·       <0.8/100,000 (Japan)

○      May increase as recognized

●      60-80% Male

○      1:1 for Head and Neck

●      Most >50 years

●      Described in most racial groups

What are the Locations of IgG4-RD?

·       Described in almost all organ systems

○      Except joints and brain parenchyma

What is the Pathophysiology of IgG4-RD?

·       IgG4 is subclass with unique structure/function

●      <5% total IgG (1.25g/L)

○      Note: Levels vary by 100 fold in healthy subjects

●      Controlled by Th2

●      Limited role in immune activation

○      Thought to be anti-inflammatory

●      Involved in other disease

○      Membranous GN

○      Pemphigus

○      TTP (Antibody against ADAMTS13 is IgG4)

●      Increasing TEM (T effector memory) cells

●      Markedly increased plasma blast compartment in flow

The 4 subclasses of human IgG were discovered in myeloma serum samples in the 1960s.12 They are named in order of abundance; IgG4 myeloma composes only 2% of IgG myeloma cases, and the reference range for serum IgG4 is approximately 0.05 to 1.5 g/L in most laboratories.13 IgG4 is generally considered an anti-inflammatory antibody, as it has a low affinity for target antigens and is unable to bind Fcγ and C1q receptors.14 While diseases such as thrombotic thrombocytopenia purpura and myasthenia gravis are mediated by IgG4 autoantibodies,15 the role of IgG4 in IgG4-RD itself requires further elucidation.16,17 Despite the prominence of IgG4-positive plasma cells in IgG4RD, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells may play a more central role in the pathophysiology of the disease.18,19

 

What are the Clinical Features of IgG4-RD?

·       Nearly any organ

●      Patients may have single organ involvement

●      Many progress to multi-organ

●      May be seen by any number of medical or surgical sub-specialists

○      Rheum, ENT, GI, Ophtho, Sg

○      Ophthalmology/ENT

■      Orbital pseudotumour

■      swelling of submandibular, parotid/lacrimal

■      Riedel’s thryoridits

■      Eosinophilic angiocentric fibrosis

○      Allergy/Pulmonary

■      Mediastinal Fibrosis

○      Renal

■      TIN

■      Membranous GN

○      Aorta/Retroperitoneal

■      Aortitis

■      Retroperitoneal fibrosis

○      GI

■      AI pancreatitis

■      Sclerosing cholangitis

○      Heme

■      Eosinophilia

■      Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia

●      Natural history is for many lesions to become fibrotic or destroy organ function

What type of disease is IgG4-RD?

UNCLEAR!

·       Autoimmune?

○      but Males>> Females

○      Low titre abs but not pathogenic

●      Inflammatory?

○      But localized to organs

○      <10% have increased CRP, IL-6

○      Fever/B-sx rare

●      Lymphoproliferative?

○      Non-clonal

○      Rarely progress to lymphoma

●      ? Process rather than disease

What is a DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH to IgG4-RD? Who to investigate?

·       Patients with ‘idiopathic’ conditions

●      Puffy glands/LN

●      Atypical Sjogren's

●      Chronic pancreatitis/biliary disease

●      Retroperitoneal/Mediastinal fibrosis

●      Eosinophilia, polyclonal gammaglobulinemia

 

What is a DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH to IgG4-RD? What to investigate with?

●      CBC, Differential

○      Eosinophilia

●      CRP

○      Normal

●      Auto-antibodies

○      May have low titre ANA

●      Proteins (Gold top tube to SPH)

○      SPEP

■      Fast-running IgG4

■      Beta-gamma bridging

■      Polyclonal band

○      IgG

○      IgG subclass

○      IgE

●      Tissue sample!!

○     

●      Imaging

○      CT head —> pelvis

■      Fibrosis, pancreatitis, masses/lymphadenopathy

What are the 6 pattern types of IgG4-RD lymphadenopathy?

 

●      Type 1: Multicentric Castleman disease-like

●      Type 2: Follicular hyperplasia

●      Type 3: Interfollicular expansion

●      Type 4: Progressive transformation of germinal center-like

●      Type 5: Inflammatory pseudotumor-like

●      Type 6: Infectious mononucleosis-like

 

What is the normal IgG4 level in serum?

 

IgG4 <1.25 g/L is normal

●      Minor elevations in IgG4 <5 g/L non-specific

●      IgG4 >5 g/L

○      95% specific

○      30% sensitive (Culvert 2014)

What are the differential diagnosis of IgG4-RD?

 

·       Non-IgG4-related diseases with elevated number of IgG4(+) cells

·       Inflammatory pseudotumor

·       Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor

·       Multicentric Castleman disease

·       Granulomatous Infections

·       Carcinoma of pancreas or cholangiocarcinoma

 

What is the Treatment for IgG4-RD?

●      Steroids

○      Prednisone 0.6mg/kg divided TID x 4weeks

○      Steroid taper, with some low dose maintenance

○      Toxicity is diabetes

■      Worsening (as have AI pancreatitis)

●      Poor Results with immunosuppressive agents

○      Imuran & Cyclosporine not helpful

●      B-cell depletion (Rituximab)

○      Carruthers Paper

■      92% achieved primary outcome (within 6 months)

■      Maintenance Rituximab may be needed

●      Immunosuppressives – azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil

●      Chemotherapy – bendamustine, rituximab

●      Novel agents – dupilumab (IL4/13), rilzabrutinib (BTK), abatacept (T-cell inhibitor), inebilizumab, obexelimab

 

How do you Monitor Response in IgG4-RD?

●      IgG4-RD RI (response index) (Carruthers Rheum Int 2012)

●      Serum IgG/IgG4

●      Novel markers

○      Plasmablasts?

Note: High levels of polyclonal hyper-gammaglobulinemia can lead to hyper-viscosity syndrome

 

 

Castleman Disease

 

 

Hyaline-vascular unicentric Castleman disease

 

Criteria

Description

Major criteria (all three required)

Enlarged lymph nodes

One enlarged lymph node (> 10 mm in the short axis diameter) or multiple enlarged lymph nodes in one lymph node station

Morphological features

Including grade 2–3 regressed follicles / hyaline-vascular follicles and:
• Prominent stroma
• Prominent high endothelial vessels
• Relatively few plasma cells

KSHV/HHV8 LANA IHC

Negative

Additional supportive histopathological features (not required)

• Variably prominent interfollicular stroma
• Compressed sinuses
• Plasmacytoid dendritic cell clusters
• No grade 2–3 plasmacytosis
• Indolent T-lymphoblastic proliferation

Other supportive features (not required)

• Mass lesion
• Lack of symptoms (in most cases)
• Co-occurring autoimmune diseases (in ~5%; paraneoplastic pemphigus, myasthenia gravis, bronchiolitis obliterans, etc.)

Exclusion criteria

• Infection: HIV, KSHV/HHV8, CMV, etc.
• Autoimmune, inflammatory, or immunodeficiency disorders: SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, etc.
• Malignancy: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, thymoma

 

Mixed/plasmacytic unicentric Castleman disease

 

Criteria

Description

Major criteria (all three required)

Enlarged lymph nodes

One enlarged lymph node or multiple enlarged lymph nodes in one lymph node station

Morphological features

Including grade 2–3 plasmacytosis; regressed follicles / hyaline-vascular follicles can be seen

KSHV/HHV8 LANA IHC

Negative

Additional supportive histopathological features (not required)

Usually includes a mix of atrophic and hyperplastic follicle features, but usually at least one regressed hyaline-vascular follicle is present

Other supportive features (not required)

• Mass lesion
• Lack of symptoms (in most cases)
• Inflammatory syndrome (in a subset)
• Constitutional symptoms
• Laboratory abnormalities including cytopenias, hypoalbuminaemia, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia, elevated CRP and/or IL-6, etc.

Exclusion criteria

• Infection: HIV, KSHV/HHV8, COVID-19, syphilis, etc.
• Autoimmune, inflammatory, or immunodeficiency disorders: SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, adult-onset Still disease, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, IgG4-related disease, etc.
• Malignancy: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, plasma cell myeloma / plasmacytoma, POEMS syndrome, etc.

Comparison of Unicentric CD vs Multicentric CD

Feature

Unicentric HV-CD

Idiopathic Multicentric CD (iMCD)

Definition

Localized benign proliferation of stromal/FDCs; single lymph node/station.

Systemic cytokine-driven disorder; ≥2 lymph node stations.

Clinical Presentation

- Asymptomatic or compressive mass (mediastinum, neck).
- Rare systemic symptoms.

- B symptoms (fever, weight loss).
- Organomegaly, edema, effusions.
- Subtypes: TAFRO or NOS.

Etiology

- Stromal/FDC dysplasia.
- VEGF dysregulation.
- Clonal stromal cells (some).

- Cytokine storm (IL-6, VEGF).
- Autoimmune/paraneoplastic triggers (unknown).

Histopathology

- Regressed GCs with hyaline-vascular lesions (lollipop/onion-skin).
- Stroma-rich variant.

- Mixed features: regressed/hyperplastic GCs + plasmacytosis (required).
- TAFRO: hypervascularity.

Diagnostic Workup

- FDC markers (CD21/CD23/CD35+).
- HHV8–.
- Rare PDGFRB mutations.

- Elevated IL-6/VEGF.
- Polyclonal plasma cells (10% monotypic).
- HHV8–.

Treatment

- Surgical excision (curative).
- Adjuvant therapy for unresectable cases.

- Anti-IL-6 (siltuximab/tocilizumab).
- Steroids, rituximab, chemotherapy for refractory cases.

Prognosis

- Excellent (rare relapse).
- Risk of FDC sarcoma.

- Poorer (5-year survival: 65%).
- TAFRO: aggressive.
- 3x malignancy risk (lymphomas).

Key DDx

- Thymoma, AITL, follicular lymphoma.

- HHV8+ MCD, POEMS syndrome, autoimmune/lymphoproliferative disorders.

 

 

January 12 - Miscellaneous Hematopathology 3

Hemochromatosis

 

Q. What is hemosiderosis?

●      Iron overload/iron deposition in tissue

Q. What is hemochromatosis?

●      Clinical expression of iron deposition in tissues

●      A generic term that refers to iron overload or accumulation of iron for any reason resulting in clinical signs & symptom

Q. What is serum Iron?

●      The amount of iron bound to transferrin

Q. What is TIBC?

●      The amount of iron that can bind to transferrin

Q. What are normal iron stores (broken down into erythrocyte, Ferritin)?

●      Erythrocyte iron (1.5-2g)

●      Ferritin or hemosiderin (600mg in female, 1 gram in men)

●      Roughly 70% of iron is incorporated in hemoglobin while the remaining 30% is stored as ferritin or hemosiderin.

●      Small quantities are also contained in serum transferrin, cytochromes and certain other enzymes.

 

Q. What is ferritin measuring?

●      Ferritin is the primary protein that stores iron within cells.

●      The quantity of serum ferritin that is present in the blood that we measure is a reflection of → the amount of total iron present in the body.

●      Ie. The protein complexed to iron, including the serum component circulating in the plasma

Q. Where are ferritin and hemosiderin primarily stored - 4 tissues?

 

●      Liver

●      Spleen

●      Bone marrow

●      Skeletal muscles

 

Q. What tubes are used for ferritin and iron?

●      Serum tubes (red or gold top)

Q. Causes of elevated Serum ferritin?

·       Hereditary conditions affecting the hepcidin/ferroportin axis:

o   HFE hemochromatosis in Caucasians

o   TFR2 hemochromatosis

o   Hemojuvelin hemochromatosis

o   Hepcidin hemochromatosis

o   Ferroportin disease

·       Conditions of ineffective erythropoiesis:

o   β-thalassemia major and intermedia

o   Hemoglobin E/β-thalassemia

o   Hemoglobin H disease

o   Congenital dyserythropoietic anemias

o   Hereditary and acquired sideroblastic anemias

·       Multiple blood transfusions:

o   Aplastic anemia

o   Diamond-Blackfan anemia

o   Thalassemia major

o   Sickle cell anemia

o   Myelodysplasia

·       Other hereditary conditions:

o   African iron overload

o   Melanesian iron overload

o   Aceruloplasminemia

o   Atransferrinemia

 

Q. What are 3 causes of secondary hemochromatosis?

●      Chronic severe hemolysis

●      Chronic/recurrent transfusion

●      Excess parenteral iron (iron poisoning)

 

Q. What are the 3 most common organs affected by hemochromatosis?

1.     Heart

2.     Liver

3.     Endocrine glands

 

Q. What are the endocrine abnormalities seen in hemochromatosis - list 4?

●      Hypogonadism

●      Hypothyroidism

●      Growth failure

●      Diabetes (“bronze diabetic”)

 

Q. What is most common severe complication of untreated hemochromatosis?

●      1/3 of patients develop hepatocellular carcinoma

 

Q. What is the gold standard for the diagnosis of hemochromatosis?

●      Assessment of the hepatic iron index (HII) is considered the "gold standard" for diagnosis of hemochromatosis.

 

Q. What are 3 other techniques that can be used to diagnose hemochromatosis?

●      Serum iron studies (ferritin, transferrin saturation)

●      HFE genetic analysis (covers approximately 80% of cases of primary hemochromatosis)

●      MRI (T2* weighted MRI - heart, ferriscan = liver)

 

Q. What is Hereditary Hemochromatosis

●      Inherited iron overload disorder

○      Excessive dysregulated intestinal iron absorption mediated at the duodenal enterocytes

○      Subtypes

·       Hemochromatosis Type 1

○      HFE gene

○      Hemochromatosis Type 2: Juvenile Hereditary Hemochromatosis:

·       Type 2A: HJV gene (hemojuvelin. Regulates hepcidin production to control iron homeostasis)

·       Type 2B: HAMP gene (hepcidin. A key hormone that inhibits iron absorption and release)

·       Hemochromatosis Type 3

○      TFR2 gene (early onset) (transferrin receptor gene. Mediates cellular uptake of iron-bound transferrin.)

·       Hemochromatosis Type 4

○      Type 4A: SLC40A1, Macrophage Type (ferroportin. Transports iron from cells (e.g., macrophages, enterocytes) into the bloodstream.)

○      Type 4B: SLC40A1, Classic Type (ferroportin)

 

 

Q. Most common gene mutated in hereditary hemochromatosis?

●      HFE (80%) → type 1 classical hereditary hemochromatosis

 

Q. What does the HFE gene do?

●      HFE is expressed on hepatocytes → helps to regulate hepcidin production.

●      A protein mutated in most cases of hemochromatosis (80%)

 

Q. What are the two common HFE mutations - which is most common?

●      The HFE gene has two common mutations, C282Y and H63D.

●      C282Y = most common

 

Q. What ethnic group has the highest incidence of hemochromatosis?

●      Approximately 10% of British, Celtic, and Scandinavian people are carriers of the C282Y mutation on the HFE gene.

 

Q. What are the rules of blood donation and hemochromatosis in Canada?

●      If you are otherwise eligible to donate blood, you can donate whole blood every 56 days.

○      Note: Women may have to respect the 84 days of normal blood donation in a woman - not truly known, but likely!

●      In between your Canadian Blood Services donations, there should be at least one week between an outpatient phlebotomy and your next donation.

●      If you have late complications from hemochromatosis such as liver cirrhosis or heart failure → you are not eligible to donate

Q. What is the general management of HH?

●      Phlebotomy (induction -> maintenance)

○      1 U (200-250 mg Fe)

■      weekly until ferritin <20-50 ng/mL and TSat <30%

■      Maintain Hct >33-35%

■      Then q2-4 months, maintain serum ferritin at ~50 ng/ml

○      Iron Chelation

○      Liver transplant

○      Testing for HCC

■      AFP/ultrasounds for high risk

●      Blood donation

○      Can give blood

■      1 week between therapeutic phlebotomy

○      Not eligible if complications!

Q. Name two other inherited iron overload disorders

·       Aceruloplasminemia (biochemical triad of mild anemia with low TSAT and high ferritin levels not due to any obvious alternative explanation)

·       Atransferrinemia

o   Absence of iron transferrin

 

 

 

TMA - Thrombotic microangiopathy

 

Q. What is the difference between TMA and MAHA?

·       MAHA: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia → a descriptive term for non-immune hemolytic anemia resulting from → intravascular red blood cell fragmentation that produces schistocytes on the peripheral blood smear.

·       TMA: Thrombotic microangiopathy → describes a specific pathologic lesion of arterioles and capillaries that leads to → microvascular thrombosis.

·       Not all MAHA is caused by a TMA → but nearly all TMAs cause MAHA (intravascular RBC fragmentation) and thrombocytopenia.

·       Acute TMA = Acute thrombocytopenia + MAHA with no other causes

 

Q. Name at least 5 disorders that are associated with MAHA and thrombocytopenia but are NOT TMAs?

·       Systemic infection

·       Systemic cancer

·       Severe hypertension

·       DIC

·       Severe preeclampsia, eclampsia, HELLP syndrome

·       Autoimmune disorders

·       Hematopoietic stem-cell or organ transplantation

These conditions are associated with intravascular RBC fragmentation (MAHA) and thrombocytopenia but NOT with the microvascular thrombosis, which is the specific pathologic lesion of arterioles and capillaries that occurs in TMA

 

Q. How are the thrombi in DIC different than in TMAs?

●      DIC → associated with microvascular thrombi that contain fibrin as well as platelets.

●      TMAs (such as TTP and HUS) → characterized by platelet rich microthrombi with reduced fibrin content (hence TMAs are associated with thrombocytopenia)

 

 

DIC thrombi

Q. What are TMAs - what are 3 common features?

●      A diverse group of disorders that can be both acquired and hereditary.

●      Defined by 3 common features of → MAHA, thrombocytopenia and organ injury.

●      Characterized by platelet rich microthrombi with reduced fibrin content.

●      Specific pathologic lesion of arterioles and capillaries that leads to microvascular thrombosis

Acquired TMA

 

Q. What are the 4 acquired TMAs?

1.     ADAMTS13 deficiency–mediated TMA (also called TTP)

2.     Shiga toxin–mediated TMA (also called ST-HUS)

3.     Drug-mediated TMA (immune reaction)

4.     Drug-mediated TMA (toxic-dose related reaction)

5.     Complement-mediated TMA (aHUS)

 

1 TTP/ADAMTS13 TMA

 

Q. What is the etiology of acquired ADAMSTS13 deficiency mediated TMA (acquired TTP)?

·       Autoantibody inhibition of ADAMTS13 activity

 

Q. What is the treatment of acquired ADAMSTS13 deficiency mediated TMA?

·       Plasma exchange

·       Immunosuppression

-        Steroids (prednisone, methylprednisolone, Rituximab)

 

Q. What is the classic pentad for TTP?

·       Fever

·       Thrombocytopenia

·       Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) = schistocytes

·       Neurological changes

·       Renal dysfunction

·       MNEMONIC: FAT RN

Q. What are the THREE categories of tests to diagnose TTP?

·       ADAMTS13 activity assay

-        Useful to establish diagnosis at disease presentation

-        Several different assay methodologies available to assess ADAMTS13 enzymatic function (e.g., ELISA, fluorescence resonance energy transfer, chemiluminescence, etc.)

-        Increased utilization of serial measurements in remission to monitor disease activity and response to therapy (immunosuppression, anti-VWF therapy)

-        Persistently decreased levels during remission correlate with increased risk of disease recurrence

·       ADAMTS13 antigen assay

-        Measures physical presence of ADAMTS13 antigen but not its functionality

-        Typically not diagnostically useful without accompanying ADAMTS13 activity assay

·       Anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies

-        Inhibiting antibodies detected by Bethesda-type mixing studies

-        Binding antibodies promote clearance and are detected by ELISA or Western blot

-        Facilitates confirmation of immune TTP as diagnosis

Q. Describe FRETS testing for TTP

·       FRETS (Fluorescence Resonance Energy Transfer Substrate) testing is a specialized assay used to diagnose Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) by measuring the activity of the enzyme ADAMTS13, which cleaves von Willebrand factor (vWF).

·       In the reagent, there is a fluorescent signal along with a quencher

·       When this is not cleaved, the fluorescence is quenched

-        With cleavage of the vWF, you get fluorescence

-        Note: need a fluorometer

 

Q. Describe the ADAMTS13 functional ELISA

·       vWF that is in the ADAMTS13 cleavage region is fixed to a plate

-        ie just a subunit of vWF

·       When you add the patient sample, cleavage of vWF occurs if there is ADAMTS13 in the sample

·       You then add an antibody that binds to the site that was cleaved that is conjugated to an enzyme

·       Addition of HRP substrate will form coloured product

·       Measure at 450/620nm spectrophotometrically

 

 

Q. Describe the ADAMTS13 Inhibitor ELISA

●      Only measure if there is a low level in the above assay

●      Mechanism

○      ADAMTS13 is bound to the plate (or beads)

○      If Antibody to ADAMTS13 is in patient plasma, it will bind to the ADAMTS13 reagent

○      Then have an Anti-human IgG antibody that recognizes the patient’s Anti-ADAMTS13 antibody

○      This antibody is conjugated an HRP

○      Substrate forms a coloured product

2 HUS TMA

 

Q. What is the etiology of HUS (shiga toxin-mediated TMA)?

·       Enteric infection with a Shiga toxin–secreting strain of Escherichia coli O157:H7 or Shigella dysenteriae.

 

Q. What is the clinical presentation and treatment of HUS?

·       Most common in children. Median age of 2.

·       Typically presents with diarrhea (bloody).

·       As the diarrhea resolves → thrombocytopenia and renal failure develop.

·       Can occur in outbreaks due to contaminated food or water or sporadically.

·       Supportive care (PLEX, ABx and immunosuppression have NO role)

 

3 DRUG TMA

 

Q. What are the 2 types of drug-mediated TMA?

·       Toxic dose related reaction

·       Immune reaction

 

Q. What is the etiology of drug-mediated TMA (toxic dose related reaction)?

·       Uncertain.

 

Q. What is the presentation and treatment of drug-mediated TMA (toxic-dose related reaction)?

·       Presentation → gradual onset of renal failure that occurs over weeks or months (as opposed to more acute in immune mediated drug TMA)

·       Treatment → removal of drug, supportive care

 

Q. What is etiology and treatment of drug mediated TMA (immune reaction) - give a classic drug example?

·       Quinine and possibly other drugs, with multiple cells affected by drug-dependent antibodies

·       Removal of drug, supportive care

 

Q. Name 5 drugs associated with drug-mediated TMA?

·       Cyclosporine

·       Quinine

·       Vincristine

·       Tacrolimus

·       Sirolimus

·       Bevacizumab

·       Gemcitabine

·       Cocaine

·       Interferon

Blood article, 2015. Drug-induced thrombotic microangiopathy: a systematic review of
published reports. Zayd et al.

 

4 COMPLEMENT TMA

 

Q. What is the etiology of acquired complement-mediated TMA?

●      Antibody inhibition of complement factor H activity

Complement activation pathways and the regulatory role of factor H.

1.     Inhibition of C3 Convertase Formation: Factor H competes with Factor B for binding to C3b, preventing the formation of the C3bBb complex (the alternative pathway C3 convertase).

2.     Dissociation of Existing Convertases: For already formed C3bBb complexes, Factor H facilitates their dissociation, stopping further amplification of the complement response.

3.     Cofactor Activity: Factor H acts as a cofactor for Factor I, an enzyme that cleaves C3b into its inactive form, iC3b. This inactivation prevents further propagation of the complement cascade.

4.     Selective Protection of Host Cells: Factor H preferentially binds to host cell surfaces via glycosaminoglycans and sialic acid. This ensures that regulatory activity is focused on self-tissues while allowing complement activation on pathogens that lack these markers.

By tightly regulating the alternative pathway, Factor H plays a critical role in preventing excessive inflammation and protecting host cells from unintended complement-mediated damage. Deficiencies or dysfunctions in Factor H are associated with diseases such as atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

Q. What is the treatment of acquired complement-mediated TMA (3)?

●      1) Plasma exchange

●      2) Immunosuppression

●      3) Anti-complement agent (eculizumab)

Congenital TMA

 

Q. What are the 4 hereditary TMAs?

●      ADAMTS13 deficiency – mediated TMA

●      Complement-mediated TMA (complement factor H, I, B, C3)

●      Metabolism-mediated TMA - MMACHC

●      Coagulation-mediated TMA - DGKE

 

Q. What is the etiology of complement mediated TMA - name at least 3 genes. Which complement pathway is deranged?

●      Mutations in → CFH, CFI, CFB, C3, CD46, and other complement genes

●      Mutations cause uncontrolled activation of → the alternative pathway of complement

 

Q. What is the clinical presentation and treatment of complement mediated TMA?

●      Presentation → initial presentation is often in children but may also be in adults; acute kidney injury is common; patients with heterozygous mutations may be symptomatic.

●      Treatment → plasma infusion or exchange, anti-complement agents

 

Q. What is the initial presentation and treatment for metabolism mediated TMA?

●      Presentation → Initial presentation is typically in children <1 year of age; also reported in one young adult with → hypertension and acute kidney injury.

●      Treatment → Vitamin supplementation: vitamin B12, betaine (amino acid compound), folinic acid

 

Q. What is the etiology of coagulation mediated TMA - what is the main gene involved?

●      Homozygous mutations in DGKE. (diacylglycerol kinase epsilon - Lipid Signaling and Platelet Activation; Endothelial Dysfunction)

●      Mutations in PLG and THBD are also potentially causative.

 

Q. How do you diagnose hereditary TTP - what 3 things must be demonstrated?

1)     Reduced ADAMTS13 activity

2)     Absence of an antibody

3)     Identification of a mutation

 

Q. Another name of cTTP

·        Upshaw-Schulman syndrome

 

Q. Plasmic score components

·       7 – Platelet, hemolysis, cancer, transplant, MCV, INR, creatinine

 

Q. What are the two types of antibodies seen in patients with acquired TTP?

●      Neutralising antibodies → that inhibit ADAMTS13 activity (most common) - block the proteolytic activity of ADAMTS13 towards VWF and are detected with in vitro functional assays.

●      Non-neutralising antibodies → that accelerate clearance of ADAMTS13 - can only be identified by enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)

 

Q. How are ADAMSTS13 neutralizing antibodies tested?

●      Mixing study

●      Perform a 1:1 mix of test:normal plasma

●      Then measure ADAMTS13 activity → presence of an inhibitor causes prolongation

 

Q. How are ADAMTS13 non-neutralizing antibodies tested?

●      Typically, by ELISA.

●      Principally, the ELISA assay detects neutralizing or non‐neutralizing antibodies against ADAMTS13. Such antibodies are predominantly of the IgG class and, to a lesser extent, of the IgM class

 

Q. What is the utility of ADAMTS13 antigen testing?

●      Limited utility.

●      Activity measurements → more informative.

●      May be normal or reduced depending on the type of antibody present.

 

Q. Give your full approach to the mechanistic classification of TMAs?

 

Acquired (4 or 5)

●      ADAMTS13 deficiency–mediated TMA (aTTP)

●      Shiga toxin–mediated TMA (also called ST-HUS)

●      Drug-mediated TMA (immune reaction)

●      Drug-mediated TMA (toxic-dose related reaction)

●      Complement-mediated TMA

Congenital (4)

●      ADAMTS13 deficiency – mediated TMA (cTTP)

●      Complement-mediated TMA

●      Metabolism-mediated TMA

●      Coagulation-mediated TMA

Amyloidosis

 

Q. What does the generic term "amyloidosis" refer to?

 

●      A generic term describing → any condition resulting in protein misfolding and deposition of amyloid fibrils in tissues.

 

Q. What is the classic definition of amyloid fibrils?

 

●      Antiparallel beta-pleated sheets on x-ray diffraction.

●      Have characteristic EM appearance and typically are identified using a combination of H&E and IHC.

ASH image bank: BM trephine Bx showing amyloid deposits intervening between cellular areas; there was apple green birefringence under polarized light

 

Q. What are the 6 most common types of amyloidosis and the protein involved

 

1.       Light chain amyloidosis (AL): Also known as primary amyloidosis. Precursor protein is monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains. Associated with plasma cell dyscrasias or mature B-cell neoplasms

2.       Secondary amyloidosis (AA): Precursor protein is serum amyloid A (SAA) protein. Reactive amyloidosis secondary to chronic inflammation, infection, certain neoplasia (renal cell ca) and familial Mediterranean fever

3.       Familial amyloidosis (FAP): Precursor protein is a variant protein such as transthyretin, fibrinogen and apolipoprotein. The most common familial amyloidosis is transthyretin-associated (ATTRm)

4.     Organ-specific: Alzheimer's is the most common. Others: skin, heart, GU

5.     Dialysis related: Protein = beta 2 microglobulin

6.     Age-related (senile) Amyloidosis: Transthyretin depositions in heart. Do better than AL amyloid in heart (75 months vs. 11 months) (ATTRwt)

Q. What are the two most common types of amyloidosis?

●      AL & AA

●      Depends on where you are in the world.

○      In western world AL is the most common

○      In some developing countries AA is more common.

Q. What are the fibrils in AA amyloidosis derived from?

●      Serum amyloid A protein in reactive (secondary, AA) amyloidosis

 

Q. Most common organ involved in AA amyloidosis?

●      Kidney → most common organ system involved in AA amyloid is the kidney (about 80 percent).

 

Q. What are the fibrils in AL amyloidosis derived from?

●      Light chains (Lambda 75% & Kappa 25%)

●      The fibrils in AL amyloidosis are derived from the variable region of lambda light chains in approximately 75 % of cases, and kappa in the remainder (25%)

 

Q. What are the 3 most common organs affected in AL and AA amyloidosis (ie most common sites of amyloid deposition)

○      1) Kidneys

○      2) Heart

○      3) Liver

 

Q. What are 5 reasons for bleeding in Amyloidosis?

●      Factor deficiency

○      Binding of factor X to the amyloid in tissues

●      Hyperfibrinolysis

●      Platelet dysfunction

●      Amyloid angiopathy

○      Friable vessels

●      Impaired vasoconstriction

Q. What are heritable amyloidosis?

●      Heterogenous group of diseases with many mutations that lead to heritable types of amyloidosis, each of which has a characteristic pattern of clinical features

 

Q. What is Age-related (senile) systemic amyloidosis?

●      Deposition of misfolded transthyretin that occurs primarily in the myocardium.

●      ATTRwt amyloidosis – Deposition of transthyretin Heart, soft tissue, nerve

●      ATTRm amyloidosis – Mutation in transthyretin Heart, kidney, soft tissue, nerve

 

Q. Compare the prognosis of AL amyloidosis with cardiac involvement vs (senile) systemic amyloidosis cardiac involvement?

●      Senile/systemic amyloidosis = more favourable

●      Patients with senile/systemic amyloidosis do much better than those with cardiac involvement by AL amyloidosis with survival of → roughly 6 years as opposed to 1.

 

Q. What is the pathogenesis in organ specific amyloidosis?

●      Amyloid deposition can occur in a single organ.

●      Typically caused by → locally produced proteins, rather than proteins that are circulating systemically.

 

Q. What is the most common type of organ specific amyloidosis?

●      Alzheimer disease → with deposition of the amyloid beta protein (Ab)

 

Q. What precursor protein undergoes misfolding in dialysis related amyloidosis?

●      Beta-2 microglobulin → in dialysis-related amyloidosis

 

Q. Describe the electron microscopy findings of amyloidosis?

●      On electron microscopy

○      8 to 10 nm in width

○      Straight and unbranching

Q. Name 5 tissue types useful to biopsy for amyloidosis. What are sensitivities of these various biopsy sites to diagnose amyloid?

●      Kidney or liver biopsy is positive in over 90 percent of cases

●      Abdominal fat pad aspirate (60-80%)

●      Rectal biopsy (50-70%)

●      Bone marrow biopsy (50-55%)

●      Skin (50%)

 

Q. What are 4 cytochemical stains that are positive in amyloid?

●      Congo red → apple-green birefringence under polarized light

●      Periodic acid-schiff positive (PAS)

●      Crystal violet positive

●      Thioflavin T positive

 

Q. What is the role of IHC in diagnosis of amyloid?

●      IHC can be used to → identify the type of protein subunit in certain cases.

●      This is most useful for AA and transthyretin (TTR) amyloid and is less so for AL amyloid.

 

Q. What is the role for mass spectrometry in a patient with amyloidosis and monoclonal serum protein?

●      Should be used to → confirm the nature of amyloid deposit.

●      In 350 patients suspected clinically of having AL amyloidosis 10% were founded to have a different type of amyloid.

●      Misdiagnosis of hereditary amyloidosis as AL (primary) amyloidosis. N Engl J Med. 2002;346(23):1786.

 

Q. What is a nuclear medicine technique that can detect amyloid deposition non-invasively?

●      Radiolabeled serum amyloid P (SAP)

●      Amyloid fibrils also bind serum amyloid P (SAP) component; this has led to the evaluation of the use of radiolabeled SAP to detect tissue amyloid deposits noninvasively

 

Q. What are 3 other substances (or co-factors) that are also deposited with all forms of amyloidosis?

●      1) Serum amyloid P component (SAP)

●      2) Glycosaminoglycans

●      3) Certain apolipoproteins (E and J)

 

Q. What is the role of the co-factors deposited in amyloidosis?

●      Uncertain role

●      Cofactors = SAP, GAGs, apolipoproteins

 

Q. General approach to treating amyloidosis?

●      Depends on the underlying cause.

●      In AL → treat the plasma cell neoplasm

●      In AA → treat the underlying infectious or inflammatory process etc.

 

Q. What is the primary differential for stromal change in the bone marrow?

●      Fibrinoid necrosis

●      Ischemic bone marrow necrosis

●      Amyloidosis

●      Gelatinous transformation of the bone marrow

●      Granulomas

●      Other causes of pale pink appearance from low power

○      cHL

○      Storage disease (Gauchers, Niemann Pick)

 

Q. How do you distinguish gelatinous transformation from amyloid by stains?

●      Gelatinous transformation → alcian blue positive

●      Amyloid → congo red positive

Q. What is light chain deposition disease?

●      A disorder where abnormal light chains are deposited in tissues secondary to a clonal plasma cell disorder.

●      The light chains do not have the same characteristics of amyloid though, and do not have the same characteristics on x-ray diffraction, EM, etc.

○      Lack the characteristic abnormal beta pleated sheet misfolded structure

 

Q. What determines if light chains will cause amyloidosis or light chain deposition disease?

●      It is uncertain.

 

Q. What are main differences between AL amyloidosis and light chain deposition diseases - complete the following table?

 

AL amyloid
