●      The tissue deposits in LCDD are usually composed of kappa light chains; they are granular not fibrillar, and do not bind Congo red, thioflavin-T, or SAP.

●      As well, the constant region of the immunoglobulin is typically deposited in this disorder.

●      Immunofluorescence microscopy is typically positive for the monoclonal light chain

 

Q. Why is immunofluorescence microscopy with anti-kappa and anti-lambda often weak or negative in amyloid deposition?

●      The fibrils in AL amyloidosis are most commonly derived from the variable region of lambda light chains.

●      The constant region is usually degraded which is what most antibodies target → therefore negative or weak staining

Draw and label an antibody

 

 

Summary - types and conditions of amyloid

 

●      AL amyloidosis → associated with plasma cell neoplasm

●      AA amyloidosis → associated with infectious or inflammatory process etc

●      Serum amyloid A protein → reactive (secondary, AA) amyloidosis

●      Age-related (senile) systemic amyloidosis → misfolded transthyretin that occurs primarily in the myocardium

●      Another substance (or co-factor) that is also deposited in all forms of amyloidosis → Serum amyloid P component (SAP)

●      Most common type of organ specific amyloidosis → Alzheimer disease → with deposition of beta protein (Ab)

●      Alzheimer disease → deposition of the beta protein (Ab)

●      Dialysis related amyloidosis → Beta-2 microglobulin

 

Additional note for beta 2 microglobulin

·       β2-Microglobulin (β2M) is a small, non-glycosylated protein (~11.8 kDa).

·       It is a component of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules, found on all nucleated cells.

·       It associates with the α-chain of MHC I and is essential for antigen presentation to CD8+ T cells.

·       Constantly shed from cell surfaces into the bloodstream.

 

A. Biomarker in Hematologic Malignancies (Multiple Myeloma, Lymphomas)

·        Elevated β2M levels are associated with increased tumor burden and poor prognosis in multiple myeloma and some lymphomas.

·        Multiple Myeloma (MM):

o            Used in the Revised International Staging System (R-ISS):

§            Stage I: β2M < 3.5 mg/L, Normal albumin, No high-risk cytogenetics.

§            Stage II: Intermediate values.

§            Stage III: β2M ≥ 5.5 mg/L → Worse prognosis.

o            High β2M reflects high tumor burden and renal dysfunction.

·        Lymphomas (e.g., Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma, CLL)

o            Elevated β2M suggests more aggressive disease and poor survival.

B. Kidney Disease and Dialysis-Related Amyloidosis (DRA)

·        β2M is cleared by the kidneys, so its levels increase in chronic kidney disease (CKD) and end-stage renal disease (ESRD).

·        Dialysis-Related Amyloidosis (DRA):

o            Long-term dialysis → β2M accumulates → forms amyloid deposits in joints and bones.

o            Symptoms: Carpal tunnel syndrome, bone cysts, joint pain.

 

Miscellaneous conditions

 

Hemophagocytic disorders in the BM (HLH)

 

What is Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)  

●      Life-threatening syndrome characterized by uncontrolled and ineffective immune response

●      Encompasses group of conditions with similar end-stage phenotype

●      Triggered in majority of cases by infection

●      Results in severe hyperinflammation → “cytokine storm”

●      Proliferation of lymphocytes &/or histiocytes in reticuloendothelial system with uncontrolled hemophagocytosis

●      May lead to multiorgan dysfunction

●      Acquired & Familial forms

Familial forms of HLH are associated with genetic mutations in what genes? What cells types are impaired by these mutations?  

●      Genetic mutations in perforin gene or in genes important for exocytosis of cytotoxic granules → that lead to impaired function of → NK and cytotoxic T cells


Acquired forms of HLH are associated with what diseases 

●      Infection (usually viral), autoimmune diseases, malignancies, and acquired immune deficiency

Age group most commonly affected?

Most common in infants from birth to 18 months of age

●      Older children and adults can also be affected

●      Usually homozygous mutations in children

What are the typical clinical manifestations of HLH   

●      Cardinal symptoms of HLH

○      Prolonged fever

○      Anemia

○      Hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy

○      Hemophagocytosis - Initially absent in significant proportion of patients

●      Other associated symptoms that may be present

○      Neurologic abnormalities

■      Cranial nerve palsy

■      Seizures in subset of patients

■      Decreased level of consciousness

○      Pulmonary infiltrate and pleural effusion

○      Cutaneous manifestations

○      Hemorrhagic maculopapular eruptions

○      Generalized erythroderma

●      Acute renal failure or multiorgan failure with severe HLH

General laboratory Findings in HLH  

●      CBC: Bi- or pancytopenia

●      Hypertriglyceridemia &/or hypofibrinogenemia

●      Hyperferritinemia and liver enzyme abnormalities

●      Hyponatremia

●      Hypoalbuminemia

What are the manifestations of the exaggerated immune response in HLH. What cells are involved? What is the cause of organomegaly & LAD?    

●      Overtly stimulated but ineffective systemic inflammatory response

●      Activation of macrophages, CD8(+) T cells, and NK cells

●      Multiorgan infiltration by activated T cells and macrophages

●      Increased cytokine production including IFN-γ, GM-CSF, and TNF-α

●      Tissue infiltration by activated T cells and macrophages results in hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy

●      High levels of cytokines, particularly IFN-γ, may lead to progressive organ failure and death in severe cases

Must you have evidence of hemophagocytosis to diagnosis HLH?  

●      No

●      Need 5 out of 8 criteria

●      Hemophagocytosis is not necessary for diagnosis

●      Diagnosis of HLH is established if 1 of the following criteria is met (A or B)

○      A) Molecular identification of mutations associated with HLH or

○      B) Detection of 5 out of 8 criteria listed below

1.     Fever

2.     Splenomegaly

3.     Cytopenia in ≥ 2 cell lines

·       Hemoglobin < 9 g/dL (< 10 g/dL if age < 4 weeks)

·       Platelets < 100 x 10⁹/L

·       Neutrophils < 1 x 10⁹/L

4.     Hypertriglyceridemia &/or hypofibrinogenemia

·       Fasting triglyceride ≥ 3 mmol/L

·       Fibrinogen < 1.5 g/L

5.     Ferritin > 500 µg/L

6.     Soluble CD25 ≥ 2,400 U/mL

7.     Decreased or absent NK cell activity

8.     Hemophagocytosis in bone marrow, CSF, or lymph nodes

 

HLH Diagnostic Criteria  

 

Why is HLH difficult to diagnoses in the early stage? 

●      May mimic ordinary infection

●      Some diagnostic symptoms may be initially missing (e.g. hemophagocytosis)

●      Other diagnostic pitfalls

○      Isolated CNS involvement

○      Fulminant liver failure, particularly in neonatal period

●      Hemophagocytosis is not necessary for diagnosis

●      Detection of infectious agent does not rule out familial HLH

Treatment options for HLH? 

●      Familial HLH is rapidly fatal disease if untreated

●      1st international treatment protocol for HLH (HLH-94 )

○      Dexamethasone and etoposide followed by cyclosporine A as maintenance therapy

○      Overall survival rate of 54%

●      HLH-2004 therapeutic protocol

○      Upfront cyclosporine A along with dexamethasone and etoposide

●      Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) in patients with genetic HLH

●      indicated to replace defective immune system with normally functioning cells

What are 4 genes mutated in familial HLH  

●      PRF1 (perforin) gene

●      UNC13D gene

●      STX11 gene

●      STXBP2 gene

Mnemonic: PUSS

What are the 5 types of familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and their associated gene mutation?   

●      FHL1: Genetic defect remains unknown at this time

●      FHL2: Linked to PRF1 (perforin) gene mutations

○      PRF1 mutations reduce or block perforin synthesis -Impairs granule-mediated cytotoxic activity of NK/T cells & inability to kill infected cells by NK cells

●      FHL3: Linked to mutations in UNC13D gene

○      UNC13D gene encodes protein that mediates exocytosis of cytotoxic granules

○      Mutation results in defective delivery of perforin and granzymes into target cells

●      FHL4: Linked to mutations in STX11 gene locus

○      STX11 gene encodes syntaxin 11 protein involved in regulation of intracellular protein transport

○      NK cells fail to degranulate when they encounter susceptible target cells

●      FHL5: Mutations in STXBP2 gene

○      STXBP2 gene encodes for syntaxin-binding protein 2

○      Involved in regulation of vesicle transport to plasma membrane

Name 4 Immune Deficiency Syndromes Associated With HLH  

●      Chediak-Higashi syndrome CHS

○      Mutations in LYST gene

●      Griscelli syndrome type 2

○      Mutations in RAB27A gene

●      Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome type 2 HPS2

○      Mutations in AP3B1 gene (aka HPS2 gene)

●      X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome XLP

○      Mutations in SH2D1A and XIAP

●      Subset of cases with severe combined immunodeficiency

●      Subset of cases with X-linked hypogammaglobulinemia

What is Macrophage activation syndrome?  

●      Form of acquired HLH associated with autoimmune diseases

●      Characterized by cytopenias, organ dysfunction, and coagulopathy associated with macrophage activation

●      Strong association with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (SJIA)

●      Markedly decreased expression of perforin on CD8(+) T and NK cells in SJIA might be responsible for macrophage activation syndrome (MAS)

●      MAS may contribute to coagulation abnormalities (DIC) in SJIA

●      Less commonly associated with other childhood rheumatic diseases including systemic lupus erythematosus

What infections are associated with acquired HLH?  

●      Viruses including

○      EBV, HSV, CMV, HIV, Parvovirus, HHV8, hepatitis viruses and Influenza (rare)

●      Bacterial-associated HLH

●      Fungal-associated HLH

●      Parasite-associated HLH

What is the most common triggering virus among viral-induced HLH? 

●      EBV

Is EBV-associated HLH More common in immunosuppressed or immunocompetent patients    

●      Most cases in immunocompetent children or adults

●      Can also occur in setting of familial and nonfamilial immune deficiencies

●      Not associated with perforin or other familial-related HLH gene mutations

In EBV-related HLH, what cells are infected with EBV  

●      CD8(+) T cells are infected with EBV

What is the general prognosis of EBV-related HLH 

●      Bad

●      Should not be considered benign condition

●      Worst prognosis compared with HLH associated with other viruses

What sort of patients develop CMV-associated HLH 

●      Healthy individuals

●      Patients with inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatologic disease, post organ transplantation

HLH Differential Diagnosis  

●      Overlapping Findings with Other Inflammatory Conditions

●      Sepsis associated with hemophagocytosis

●      Severe inflammatory response syndrome

●      Multiorgan dysfunction syndrome

What is most common underlying disease in Parvovirus-associated HLH  

●      Hereditary spherocytosis

What is the general prognosis of Parvovirus B19-associated HLH  

●      Good

●      B19-associated HLH carries better prognosis compared to other virus-associated HLH

3 e.g.s of bacteria causing Bacterial-associated HLH  

●      Mycobacteria, BCG therapy, and BCG vaccination

●      Campylobacter, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Salmonella typhi, Rickettsia, Ehrlichia, and Borrelia (Lyme disease)

3 e.g.s of fungi causing Fungal-associated HLH  

●      Candida, Cryptococcus, Pneumocystis, Histoplasma, and Aspergillus

●      Common in setting of AIDS, transplant recipients, and lymphoma

3 e.g.s of parasites causing Parasite-associated HLH  

Leishmania, malaria, Toxoplasma, Babesia (babesiosis), and Strongyloides stercoralis

What malignancies are associated with acquired HLH? 

●      Lymphomas and leukemias

●      T-/NK-cell lymphomas/leukemias, anaplastic large cell lymphoma, plasma cell myeloma

●      Monocytic leukemias, acute lymphoblastic leukemia

●      Solid tumors

○      Germ cell tumor, thymoma, carcinoma

HHV8-associated HLH usually occurs in the setting of what 2 diseases?     

●      Most cases in setting of Kaposi sarcoma or multicentric Castleman disease

●      Rarely reported in renal transplant recipients

Molecular Testing in Suspected HLH: what genes would you test for?     

●      Gene panel using next-generation sequencing, including

●      Genes involved in familial HLH

○      PRF1, UNC13D, STX11, and STXBP2 (PUSS)

●      Genes involved in immune deficiency syndromes associated with HLH

○      LYST, RAB27A, AP3B1, SH2D1A, and XIAP

Q. HLH mechanism?

 

-        Uncontrolled proliferation of activated lymphocytes and macrophages

-        Characterized by proliferation of morphologically benign lymphocytes and macrophages that → secrete high amounts of inflammatory cytokines.

-        Classified as → “cytokine storm syndrome”

 

Q. What are the types (classification) of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis? 

 

-        1) Primary, also known as congenital → a group of rare autosomal recessive (AR) disorders that usually present early in life but can have delayed presentation

-        2) Secondary, also known as acquired, → is more common in adults

 

Q. How does HLH present?

 

-        Patients are quite sick

-        Most patients with HLH are acutely ill with → multiorgan involvement.

-        Common findings include → fever, hepatosplenomegaly, rash, lymphadenopathy, neurologic symptoms, cytopenias, high serum ferritin, and liver function abnormalities.

 

Q. What are the HLH diagnostic criteria for acquired (non-congenital) HLH?

 

1)     Molecular diagnosis c/w HLH, or

2)     Require 5 out of 8

1)     Fever

2)     Splenomegaly

3)     Cytopenias affecting at least 2 of three lineages (hgb <90, plt<100, neuts<1)

4)     Ferritin >500

5)     Hypertriglyceridemia (>3.0mmol/L) and/or hypofibrinogenemia (< 1.5)

6)     Hemophagocytosis in bone marrow or other tissues

7)     Low or absent NK cell activity

8)     Soluble CD25 (sIL-2 receptor) >2400U/ml

 

Q. How do you diagnose congenital HLH?

 

Molecular diagnosis of the five subtypes based on their known gene mutations

-        PRF1 (Perforin) (most common gene affected)

-        UNC13D

-        STX11

-        STXBP2

-        HPLH1

-        “PUSS” mnemonic = PRF1, UNC13D, STX11, STXBP2 (plus H - for HLH)

-        Perfect! University of North Carolina Strix 11 points and 2 Bonus Points.

 

 

Most cases are due to homozygous perforin mutations.

Q. Is a heterozygous gene mutation sufficient for diagnosis of HLH?

-        In children need homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations.

-        In adults in appropriate clinical context a heterozygous mutation can be supportive.

 

Q. What are some infectious agents HLH is associated with - give 4 egs?

-        EBV

-        Parvo B19

-        Babesia microti

-        Cryptococcus neoformans

-        From Eman: EBV, CMV, HSV, parvovirus B19, human herpes virus 6, adenovirus, and varicella zoster virus, PCR is recommended over serology

-        Visceral leishmaniasis

 

Q. What immunodeficiency disorders are associated with HLH, and what are their genes - give 4 egs?

 

-        Chediak Higashi syndrome (LYST[QZ2] )

-        Griscelli Syndrome type 2 (RAB27A[QZ3] )

-        Hermansky Pudlak Syndrome type 2 (HPS-2[QZ4] )[AP3B1 by Blood How I Treat]

-        Subset of SCID (RAG1 & 2[QZ5] )[IL2RG by Blood How I Treat]

-        X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome (SH2D1A and XIAP[QZ6] )[SH2D1A XLP typ1, BIRC4/XIAP XLP type 2 by Blood How I Treat]

-        Subset of X-linked hypogrammaglobulinemia

 

What are acquired causes of HLH?

-        Infection - EBV (most classic), cryptococcus neoformans, Parvovirus B19, Babesia, HIV, TB

-        Auto-inflammatory/ Macrophage activation syndrome

-        Malignancy

-        Immunosuppression

-        Metabolic

 

Q. What is the role of assessment of CSF in HLH - what are you looking for?

-        HLH may cause → meningoencephalitis and significant neurological sequelae.

-        CSF analysis is to assess for elevated lymphocytes and/or proteins.

-        It is not to assess for hemophagocytosis.

 

Q. What is the incidence of HLH BM involvement?

-        The reported incidence of hemophagocytosis in bone marrow examination ranges from 25 to 100 percent

 

Q. What is a bone marrow finding other than hemophagocytosis consistent with HLH?

-        Infiltration of the BM by → activated macrophages, if seen, is also consistent with HLH.

 

Q. What are the treatment options in HLH?

-        Newer regiment called → HLH-2004 as well

-        Etoposide, Dexamethasone Cyclosporine

-        For refractory disease and those with HLH gene mutations can use allogeneic SCT.

-        Excellent Blood how I treat article on HLH that is worthwhile to review. https://doi.org/10.1182/blood-2015-01-551622

 

What is the goal of treatment for HLH?

 

-        Goal is to halt any trigger and control the immune system

-        Disease specific treatment if malignancy or infection is identified

-        Primary - BM transplant

-        Secondary eg if lymphoma-associated HLH:

-        Use etoposide-containing chemotherapy (10mg/kg) then taper

-        Dexamethasone

-        Cyclosporine, IVIg

-        Additional immunosuppressive therapy should be initiated immediately in severe cases and in those that fail to respond to disease-specific therapy after 2 to 3 days.

-        If no clear precipitant, or if EBV infection, then start etoposide regimen ASAP

Collagen Vascular Disorders, Hematologic Manifestations of

 

(This seems pretty low yield… not very many specific features, basically on the differential for other things)

Collagen vascular disorder include?

·        Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)

·        Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

·        Polymyositis/dermatomyositis

·        Scleroderma

·        Polymyalgia rheumatica

·        Sjögren syndrome

What BM histologic features may be present in CVD?    

●      Cellularity

○      Highly variable, ranging from hypocellular to hypercellular

●      Bony trabeculae abnormalities

○      Present in ~ 35% of cases

○      Variable, osteopenic or osteosclerotic abnormalities can be seen

●      Lymphoid aggregates

○      Common but nonspecific

○      Also observed in normal individuals, incidence increases with age

●      Lipogranulomas

●      Sea-blue histiocytes

○      May be more specific finding, but only rarely seen

●      Megaloblastic changes in erythroid lineage

○      Mild to severe

○      ~ 30% of cases

○      Nonspecific

○      Differential diagnostic considerations include vitamin B12 &/or folate deficiency, myelodysplastic syndrome, other

●      Abnormal localization of immature precursors

○      Immature granulocytes located away from bony trabeculae and blood vessels

○      ~ 20% of cases

○      Also seen in myelodysplastic syndrome

●      Methotrexate-induced lymphoproliferative disorders

○      Other secondary neoplasms also occur

●      Lymphocytes

○      Quantitation of B and T lymphocytes is highly variable

○      Can be decreased, normal, or increased

●      Usually minimal fibrosis but can be associated with autoimmune myelofibrosis (secondary)

DDx for CVD changes in the BM?    

●      Myelodysplastic Syndromes

○      Must exclude reactive causes of cytopenias/dysplasia

○      Cytogenetic abnormalities or other evidence of clonality helpful

○      Significantly increased blasts not seen in CVD

○      Multilineage dysplasia not seen in CVD

●      Myeloproliferative Neoplasms

○      May have JAK2 or other genetic mutations or chromosomal abnormalities

●      Autoimmune Myelofibrosis

○      Primary; not associated with CVD

○      Morphologically indistinguishable from secondary forms that are associated with CVD

○      Requires clinical work-up to evaluate for associated CVD

○      Diffuse bone marrow fibrosis with lymphoid aggregates

○      Benign clinical course

●      Vitamin B12 &/or Folate Deficiency

○      Exclude with laboratory evaluation for serum vitamin B12 and folate

●      Alcohol Abuse

○      Clinical history critical

○      Frequently accompanying liver disease

●      Viral Infections

○      Hepatitis C virus with liver disease most common

○      Exclude with serologic or molecular work-up or known history

●      Medications

○      Can mimic CVD bone marrow

○      Chemotherapeutic agents

○      Antiretroviral agents

○      Anticonvulsants

○      Arsenic

 

 

Chronic Renal Disorders, Hematologic Manifestations of

 

Hematologic and bone marrow consequences of CRD consist of 2 primary categories     

●      Anemia of CRF

●      Renal osteodystrophy


What are the multifactorial causes of Chronic anemia associated with Chronic Renal Disorders     

●      Anemia due to decreased erythropoietin production by kidney (main factor)

●      Insufficient available iron to support erythropoiesis (functional iron deficiency from many causes)

○      Iron (blood) loss in hemodialysis

○      Iron malabsorption

○      GI blood loss (telangiectasias)

●      Suppression of erythropoiesis in bone marrow (uremic toxic, cytokine effects)

●      Decreased red blood cell survival time (linked to uremia)

●      Concurrent anemia of chronic disease picture from chronic infection/inflammation

●      Microangiopathy (hemolytic uremic syndrome picture)

●      Dilutional anemia from increased plasma volume

●      Aluminum toxicity

●      Folate deficiency


What are the causes of Renal Osteodystrophy     

●      Maintenance of normal bone remodeling impaired in CRD

●      Low and high bone turnover rates

●      Effects of secondary hyperparathyroidism

●      Defective bone mineralization


Lab tests useful to work up renal osteodystrophy     

●      Assessment for renal osteodystrophy

○      Standard tests for bone homeostasis

○      Hyperparathyroidism assessment

○      Vitamin D, aluminum levels

○      Osteomalacia assessment

●      Anemia assessment

●      CBC, RBC parameters, reticulocyte count, iron measurements

●      Inflammatory cytokine levels/hepcidin

Treatment options for anemia of CRD     

●      Erythropoiesis stimulating factors/human recombinant EPO

○      Significant improvement in anemia typical

○      Some patients develop red cell aplasia from anti-EPO antibodies

○      Some patients become EPO resistant

●      Dialysis required for many patients

Blood film findings anemia of CRD     

●      Normocytic/normochromic anemia with variable, often reduced polychromasia

●      May see Burr cells/echinocytes

●      Rare cases exhibit fragments, schistocytes, and spherocytes (hemolytic uremic syndrome picture)

●      White blood count variable

●      Platelets usually normal in number and morphology

BM film findings anemia of CRD

●      Bone marrow examination not generally necessary

●      Highly variable features dependent on

○      Duration of CRD

○      Type and severity of renal osteodystrophy

○      Anti-EPO antibody-induced red cell dysplasia (rare)

●      Assess bony trabeculae (BT) and bone marrow stroma for

○      Width of BT (osteopenia/osteosclerosis)

○      Osteoblast rimming/number

○      Number of osteoclasts

○      Extent of mineralization of bone

○      Bone islands

○      Associated fibrosis

Lysosomal Storage Diseases With Predominantly Histiocytic Storage

Overview

3 groups of lysosomal storage disease    

●      1) Lysosomal Storage Diseases with Predominantly Histiocytic Storage

○      These differ morphologically and clinically from the other 2 groups

●      2) Lysosomal storage diseases associated more exclusively with abnormalities of leukocyte granulation

●      3) Storage diseases with predominantly soft tissue or organ-based pathology

Definitive diagnosis of Lysosomal Storage Diseases with Predominantly Histiocytic Storage can be achieved using what 2 tests?  

1)     Clinical presentation

○      Differs by storage disease subtype

○      Useful in directing testing

2)     Microscopic findings

○      May help to direct enzymatic testing

○      Usually not independently diagnostic

3)     Enzymatic analysis

○      Peripheral blood leukocytes or

○      Cultured fibroblasts

4)     Molecular analysis

○      May be used for confirmation or for carrier testing

4 examples of Lysosomal Storage Diseases with Predominantly Histiocytic Storage

1.     Gaucher disease

2.     Niemann-Pick disease

3.     Mucolipidosis I (Sialidosis)

4.     Cystinosis

5.     Fucosidosis

6.     Farber

7.     Fabry

Top Differential Diagnoses for Lysosomal Storage Diseases with Predominantly Histiocytic Storage - give 5 differentials

●      Pseudo-Gaucher cells and reactive sea-blue histiocytes

○      Seen in setting of rapid cellular turnover

■      eg. seen with CML, MM and hemoglobinopathies

■      Usually minor population on aspirate smear (in contrast to most storage diseases, where they are abundant)

●      Other conditions associated with histiocytic infiltration

○      Infection

○      Langerhans cell histiocytosis or other neoplastic histiocytosis

○      Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis

What is the lysosome? And what is its function?

·       Cytoplasmic organelle containing enzymes

·       Enzymes degrade a variety of compounds

·       Proteins, DNA/RNA, carbohydrates, lipids

o   Active at low pH

o   Acidic pH maintained via proton pump

What are Lysosomal Storage Diseases?

·       Heterogeneous group of rare genetic disorders

·       Genetic defects in

o   Lysosomal acid hydrolase (enzyme)

o   Membrane protein

o   Transporter

·       Progressive accumulation of enzyme substrate within lysosomes

o   Interfere with cellular and tissue function

What is the inheritance of LSD?

·       1 in 7000-8000 births

·       Mostly Autosomal recessive

·       Few X-linked

Which ethnicities get LSD?

·       Higher incidence in Ashkenazi Jewish, likely founder effect

Name 4 types of LSD?

·       Gaucher

·       Tay-Sachs

·       Niemann-Pick

·       Mucolipidosis IV

 

What is the most common LSD?

·       Gaucher Disease

·       1 in 75,000 births

1.Gaucher Disease

Key features of Gaucher Disease:

Feature

Details

Pattern of Inheritance

Autosomal recessive

Gene Mutated

GBA gene

Enzyme Deficiency

Acid β-glucocerebrosidase (ABG=GBA gene)

Substrate

Glucocerebroside

Function of Enzyme

Breaks down glucocerebroside into glucose and ceramide

Pathology

Glucocerebroside accumulates in macrophages, forming Gaucher cells

Q. What is Gaucher disease?

-        A disorder in which glucocerebroside accumulates in certain cells and tissues.

-        It is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase.

 

Q. What are the clinical features?

-        Hepatosplenomegaly with hypersplenism and pancytopenia/cytopenias.

-        Neurologic symptoms are common in type II and type III as well.

 

Q. What are the genetics of this disorder?

-        Different mutations in the GBA (beta-glucosidase) gene determine the remaining activity of the enzyme.

-        It is an autosomal recessive disorder.

-        Over 80 mutations that result in 3 different clinical phenotypes = no specific gene mutation to know

-        Think of the “G’s” going together

-        GBA gene mutation

-        Glucocerebrosidase enzyme deficiency

-        Glucocerebroside substrate accumulation

-        Gaucher disease

 

Q. How is Gaucher disease treated?

1.     Recombinant glucocerebrosidase (Imiglucerase)

2.     Substrate reduction therapy (Miglustat - crosses BBB)

 

Q. Gaucher's disease has an increased incidence of what hematological neoplasm?    

·       Plasma cell myeloma

 

Q. Classic Gaucher's disease macrophage morphology?

·       Tissue paper like macrophages

 

 

●      Image: ASH image bank


 

What are 5 causes of Massive Splenomegaly

1.     Chronic myeloid leukemia

2.     Myelofibrosis, primary or secondary to polycythemia vera or essential thrombocytosis

3.     Lymphoma, usually indolent, including hairy cell leukemia

4.     Gaucher disease

5.     Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis)

6.     Hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly syndrome, also called tropical splenomegaly syndrome

7.     Beta thalassemia major or severe beta thalassemia intermedia

8.     AIDS with Mycobacterium avium complex

 

What are the 3 types of Gaucher’s?

·       Type I: Most common type, 60% diagnosed before age 20; no CNS involvement (nonneuronopathic)

o   Leu444Pro is most common genotype

o   More severe disease

·       Type II (acute): Primary neurologic disease with onset before age 2; rapidly progressive with death by age 2-4

·       Type III (subacute/chronic): Similar to type II with CNS disease but slowly progressive

 

What is the clinical course of Gaucher?

·       Presents perinatal to adulthood

·       Varying degrees of severity

·       Lethal to asymptomatic

 

What are the hematological manifestations of Gaucher?

·       Thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy

·       Anemia

·       Splenomegaly

·       Gammopathies and malignancy

 

What is the classic bone deformity associated with Gaucher?

·       Erlenmeyer flask deformity

 

 

How many types of Gaucher disease are there? What are their clinical manifestations?

●      1) Type I (nonneuronopathic)

○      Bone disease

○      Cytopenias (anemia, thrombocytopenia)

○      Hepatosplenomegaly

○      Lung disease

●      Types II and III (acute neuronopathic)

○      Mostly as above, but with prominent CNS manifestations

●      Type III shows somewhat later onset than type II (chronic neuronopathic)

Laboratory Tests in Gaucher disease

●      Diagnosis of symptomatic patients rests on assessment of β-glucocerebrosidase / β-glucosylceramidase enzyme activity

●      Often performed on peripheral blood leukocytes

●      Affected individuals show enzymatic activity < 15% of normal

●      Targeted mutation analysis available for high-risk populations (e.g., Ashkenazi Jews)

●      Most useful for carrier screening → skin fibroblasts

Treatment of Gaucher disease

●      Enzyme replacement therapy

●      Recombinant glucosylceramidase is bioavailable for cellular uptake and can ameliorate symptoms

●      Substrate reduction therapy

●      Bone marrow transplant for some subtypes

Histologic Features of Gaucher disease? Two stains?

●      Characteristic Gaucher cells

●      Histiocytes with delicately wrinkled cytoplasm, resembling tissue paper

●      Positive for PAS and TRAP (the Hairy cell leukemia stain)

 

2.Niemann Pick Disease

Key Features of Niemann-Pick Disease

Feature

Details

Pattern of Inheritance

Autosomal recessive

Genes Mutated

Types A & B: SMPD1(Sphingomyelin Phosphodiesterase 1); Type C: NPC1 or NPC2

Enzyme Deficiency

Types A & B: Acid sphingomyelinase (ASM); Type C: Cholesterol transport proteins

Substrate

Types A & B: Sphingomyelin
Type C: Cholesterol and glycolipids

Function of Enzyme

ASM: Breaks down sphingomyelin
NPC1/2: Transport cholesterol in lysosomes

Pathology

Accumulation of sphingomyelin (Types A & B) or cholesterol (Type C) in lysosomes

Clinical Features

Type A: Infantile neurodegeneration, hepatosplenomegaly, cherry-red macula
Type B: Hepatosplenomegaly, lung disease, mild/no neuro symptoms
Type C: Ataxia, dystonia, hepatosplenomegaly, psychiatric symptoms

Histologic Features

Foam cells, sea-blue histiocytes, vacuolated lymphocytes

Q. What is Niemann-Pick Disease?

·       Disorder in which sphingomyelin accumulates in the lysosomes of cells.

·       Deficiency of sphingomyelinase

 

3 types of Niemann Pick disease and their clinical manifestations

●      Types A/B are distinguished by age of onset and severity

○      Type A: Severe progressive neurodegenerative symptoms in 1st year of life (neuronopathic)

○      Type B: Chronic progressive visceral form of disease (nonneuronopathic)

■      Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, interstitial lung disease, joint pain, coronary artery disease

■      Liver disease (40%) manifests as fulminant liver failure or cirrhosis

■      Variant form of type B has neurologic manifestations

●      Type C presentation varies with age

○      Pre- or perinatal period: Cholestatic jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, acute liver failure, and pulmonary disease

○      Infantile or juvenile period (2-15 years): Neurologic manifestations, hepatosplenomegaly, and history of neonatal cholestasis

○      Adults (> 15 years): Psychiatric illness and cognitive impairment, neurologic manifestations, or visceral signs, such as hepatomegaly and splenomegaly

○      Visceral manifestations may be less prominent or asymptomatic in adults

Q. What are the heme related clinical issues?

·       Main heme related ones are hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia.

 

Lab tests in Niemann-Pick (types A and B)

●      Enzymatic assay for acid sphingomyelinase activity for diagnosis of affected individuals

●      Molecular analysis of SMPD1 for confirmation &/or carrier detection

Histologic Features of Niemann-Pick disease

●      Histiocytes with expanded cytoplasm filled with innumerable small to coarse vacuoles

○      Foam cells




●      Some cases show admixed (or even predominant) sea-blue histiocytes

○      Histiocytes with granular, dark blue cytoplasm

○      Contain undegraded ceroid

●      Sea-blue histiocytes can also be present in other storage diseases (Fabry disease, ceroid storage disease, lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase deficiency, acid lipase deficiency, etc.)

●      Vacuolated lymphocytes (some subtypes)

●      Foamy macrophages

 

 

●      Sea-blue histiocytes

 

Q. What is the treatment?

-        No specific treatment exists.

Key features of Mucolipidosis I (Sialidosis):

Feature

Details

NEU1

4.Cystinosis胱氨酸贮积症

Key features of Cystinosis:

Feature

Details

Pattern of Inheritance

Autosomal recessive

Gene Mutated

CTNS

Protein Deficiency

Cystinosin (lysosomal cystine transporter protein)

Substrate That Accumulates

Cystine (trapped in crystallized form within lysosomes)

Function of Protein

Exports cystine out of lysosomes into the cytoplasm

Pathology

Accumulation of cystine crystals within lysosomes, causing cellular damage

Treatment of Cystinosis

●      Cysteamine bitartrate

●      Cystine-depleting agent that can prevent primary complications

Histologic Features of Cystinosis 

●      Histiocytes packed with polarizable cystine crystals

●      May be dissolved by water-based fixation (and therefore missed on histologic examination)

Bone marrow transplant has been effective in which Lysosomal Storage Diseases with Predominantly Histiocytic Storage

●      Niemann-Pick disease (types B and C)

●      Plus others

Erdheim-Chester disease

What is Erdheim-Chester disease?

●      A rare disease characterized by → abnormal proliferation of histiocytes, or tissue macrophages (non-Langerhans-cell histiocytosis)

●      Characterized by:

○      Infiltration of → lipid-laden macrophages, multinucleated giant cells, an inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes and histiocytes in the bone marrow

○      Pancytopenia

○      Generalized sclerosis of the long bones

○      Hepatosplenomegaly

●      aka Erdheim-Chester syndrome or polyostotic sclerosing histiocytosis

●      Disseminated juvenile xanthogranuloma is similar pediatric entity

○      Non-LCH, associated with juvenile chronic myelogenous leukemia (JMML), presents as a solitary red-brown, yellowish papule or nodule, most often on the head and neck area

 

Some of the memorizing tips.

Tay-Sachs disease: the 6 (hexo) gang (a group of guys from the six, toronto or gang of 6 guys ie. ganglioside) eats some onions (onion-skin) and cherries (cherry-red spot) and puts some in their sacks (tay-sachs) - i imagine a group of guys eating onions and cherries and packing them in bags

Fabry disease: the alpha girl (a-galactosidase and X-linkage ie. girl has two X) makes ceramics (ceramide) and fabrics (Fabry), hurts her fingers (peripheral neuropathy) and/but doesn't sweat (hypohidrosis), bites her lip bleeding (angiokeratomas) from the focus - i imagine a girl super focused on arts and crafts.

MCLD: Real sulfate (arylsulfatase A & sulfate ie. yellow ie. chromatic) affects the cerebrum with dementia, demyelination, ataxia - this was a bit not-so-straightforward, but i would imagine blobs of yellow affecting CNS, kind of like kernicterus if that makes sense. i hope you get a hang of this with the rest!

Gaucher disease: Gals/girls (galacto-) from across the globe (globoid cells) eat crabs (Krabbe) with big eyes (optic atrophy) that destruct, ie. with crab claws, oligodendrocytes

Niemann-Pick disease: Sphingers/fingers (sphingomyelinase) pick cherries (Pick & cherry-red spot) from whipped cream foam (foam cells; also helpful if you speak arabic, famm means mouth ie. reference to eating) and they accumulate in the stomach (causing HSM)

Hurler syndrome: I do run in days (iduroniase) so fast as a gargoyle (gargoylism). I didn't see anything (corneal clouding) and my stomach hurt (from HSM) but I hepaRAN (heparan & ran out of breath ie. airway obstruction) so I'm not killed (ie. not a hunter but a prey)

Hunter syndrome: As a hunter I am aggressive and I see clearly (no corneal clouding) to hit the X (the goal of the hunter ie. X linked) but I do run to (hunter runs to the prey to attack) the sulfatase (i do run 2 sulfatase ie. iduronate-2-sulfatase) to catch it (ie. hunter)

What is gelatinous transformation? What is the BM stroma?   

●      Altered BM stroma composed of hyaluronic acid with increased glycosaminoglycan

●      aka Serous fat atrophy, gelatinous atrophy or degeneration

Microscopic features of Gelatinous transformation

●      Homogeneous eosinophilic stroma with atrophic adipocytes and decreased hematopoiesis

●      Core biopsy may show focal, patchy, or diffuse pattern



Name 4 conditions associated with gelatinous transformation of the BM

1.     Malignancy (both hematolymphoid and metastatic)

2.     Malnutrition (including alcoholism and anorexia nervosa)

3.     Maldigestive conditions

4.     Infections (particularly AIDS)

5.     Heart failure, metabolic disorders

Causes of fibrinoid necrosis?

·       Seen following myeloablative chemotherapy

Microscopic features of Fibrinoid necrosis

·       Eosinophilic granular stroma with net-like appearance

In Fibrinoid necrosis, the stromal material stains positive for?

·       Fibrinogen and hyaluronidase

Cause of Ischemic (coagulative) necrosis

·       Occurs secondary to vascular insufficiency = infarction eg SSD


 

Name 4 conditions associated with Ischemic (coagulative) necrosis

1.     Malignancy (particularly acute leukemia)

2.     Sickle cell anemia

3.     Graft-vs-host disease

4.     Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

5.     DIC or infection

Ischemic bone marrow necrosis commonly manifests with what symptoms?

●      Bone pain, fever, fatigue, jaundice

Abnormal lab results with ischemic bone marrow necrosis

●      Cytopenias

○      Anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia

●      Markers of cell injury

○      Elevated lactate dehydrogenase, elevated alkaline phosphatase

Microscopic features of Ischemic necrosis of medullary cavity alone or with bone

●      Sections show granular matrix with ghost cells

●      Necrotic bone will show loss of osteocytes

Aspirate smear findings with Ischemic necrosis of BM

●      Show cells with indistinct nuclear and cytoplasmic membranes in background of homogeneous basophilic granular material

Peripheral blood findings with Ischemic necrosis of BM

●      May show pancytopenia, leukoerythroblastic blood picture, or (rarely) microangiopathic hemolytic anemia

Reticulin fibers are normal component of bone marrow stroma typically associated with what 3 structures  

●      Sinuses, large vessels, and lymphoid aggregates

What material is deposited in pathologic BM fibrosis 

●      Collagen fibers and increased reticulin fibers are pathologic

●      Collagen = irreversible

●      Reticulin = reversible



Increased reticulin fibers and any detectable collagen fibers are pathologic and may be induced by what factors - give 3 egs?

Growth factors

●      Transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β)

●      Platelet-derived growth factor

●      Interleukin-1 (IL-1)

●      Substance P

●      Basic fibroblast growth factor

●      Epidermal growth factor

●      Vascular endothelial growth factor

Microscopic features of BM fibrosis - what 2 stains are used for visualization? Describe how you do the stain?

●      Silver stain: subtle to marked increase in reticulin fibers best visualized by silver stains (reticulin stain)

○      Oxidise → in acidified potassium permanganate = active component of the dye

○      Decolourise → with oxalic acid

○      Impregnate → in ammoniacal silver solution

○      No counterstain

●      Trichrome stain: severe fibrosis is associated with deposition of thick collagen fibers (positive by trichrome stain)

○      Masson’s trichrome

●      May impart streaming quality to associated marrow cells

●      Often accompanied by neovascularization and dilated sinuses

What abnormal cells may release factors contributing to fibrosis

●      Apoptotic megakaryocytes

●      Growth factor release from alpha granules

What is amyloid protein? 

●      Deposition of abnormally folded proteins with high β-pleated sheet content

●      A generic term describing → any condition resulting in protein misfolding and deposition of amyloid fibrils in tissues.

Name 4 conditions associated with BM amyloid deposition

●      Primary systemic amyloidosis (AL)

●      Plasma cell myeloma

●      Waldenström macroglobulinemia/lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma

●      Chronic inflammatory states (AA amyloidosis)

Which type of amyloid occurs with primary systemic amyloidosis

●      AL

Which type of amyloid occurs with chronic inflammatory states   

●      AA amyloidosis

Microscopic BM features of Amyloid deposition. Name 4 stains that will be positive! 

●      Sections show homogeneous eosinophilic deposits in vessel walls and, less commonly, interstitium

●      Positive with PAS, crystal violet, thioflavin T, and Congo red stains

○      JQ notes have the same 4 stains

●      Congo red stain reveals characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarization, or salmon pink material under normal light microscopy

Microscopic aspirate features of Amyloid deposition

●      Aspirate smears show homogeneous eosinophilic to dark purple waxy globules

●      Thickened blood vessels

●      Bone marrow smear showed multiple cloud-like, fluffy texture of the deposits. (ASH)

 

Electron microscopy features of BM Amyloid deposition

●      Sows characteristic 10-nm fibrils but is rarely necessary

●      Antiparallel beta-pleated sheets on x-ray diffraction

What does cystinosis look like?

 

Cystinosis clinical manifestations in early-onset classic disease - 2 features?

  1. Renal Fanconi Syndrome:
    • Proximal renal tubular dysfunction causing:
      • Polyuria (excessive urination) and polydipsia (excessive thirst).
      • Electrolyte imbalances (hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hypocalcemia).
      • Metabolic acidosis (due to bicarbonate wasting).
      • Glycosuria (glucose in urine) and aminoaciduria (amino acid loss).
  1. Failure to Thrive/Growth Retardation:
    • Impaired growth due to chronic electrolyte losses, malnutrition, and renal wasting of nutrients.

Cause of primary hyperoxaluria    

●      Enzyme deficiencies cause → excess oxalate production

What do you see in the bone marrow in hyperoxaluria?

●      Calcium oxalate crystals are seen in primary hyperoxaluria

○      A group of rare metabolic disorders with AR inheritance.

●      Excess oxalate forms insoluble calcium salts in bone marrow and other tissues.

○      Bone is the largest repository for excess oxalate.

●      Calcium oxalate crystals appear as unstained rhomboidal-shaped or needle-shaped crystals that range from 200-300 μm in length and form rosettes or star-like figures.

●      Crystals may also be isolated or grouped in clusters.

Below: Calcium oxalate crystals H&E under normal light, and polarized light

 

Oxalosis clinical manifestations - give 3

●      Recurrent kidney stones, nephrocalcinosis

●      Urinary tract infections

●      Renal failure

●      Widespread tissue deposition of calcium oxalate crystals after renal damage

Cause of Crystal-storing histiocytosis

●      Usually excess κ-light chains form crystals

●      Rare non-immunoglobulin variants


Crystal-storing histiocytes may be associated with what disorders

●      90% associated with plasma cell dyscrasia or lymphoproliferative disorder

●      May see crystals in plasma cells or lymphocytes

Charcot-Leyden crystals are the morphologic hallmark of

●      Eosinophil-related disease

Hemoglobin C crystals may occur in 3 disease scenarios

●      Hemoglobin C disease

●      Hemoglobin SC disease

●      Hemoglobin C/β-thalassemia

What is this type of crystal?

●      Charcot-Leyden crystals

Charcot-Leyden Crystals: Key Features

Feature

Details

Composition

They consist of protein aggregates of lysolecithin acylhydrolase, a breakdown product of eosinophils.

Origin

Formed from eosinophil breakdown in tissues or fluids

Morphology

Crystals vary in size (up to 50 µm in length) and are slender, often with pointed ends.

Associated Conditions

Eosinophil-related diseases with active eosinophilic inflammation or proliferation, including:

- Allergic diseases (asthma, allergic rhinitis)

- Parasitic infections

- Eosinophilic pneumonia, eosinophilic gastroenteritis

- Hematologic disorders (eosinophilic leukemia, hypereosinophilic syndrome)

Staining

Can be seen on Wright-Giemsa stain or in histologic sections

 

Bone Abnormalities in Bone Marrow Specimens

Term

Definition

Causes

Osteopenia

Lower than normal bone mineral density, but not severe enough for osteoporosis.

Aging, hormonal changes, poor nutrition, sedentary lifestyle.

Osteoporosis

Progressive bone disease with decreased density and increased fracture risk.

Aging, hormonal imbalances, chronic steroid use, certain medical conditions.

Osteolysis

Pathological destruction or resorption of bone tissue.

MM

ATLL

Systemic mastocytosis

Basophilic leukemia

Langerhans cell histiocytosis

Erdheim Chester disease

Osteonecrosis

Death of bone tissue due to lack of blood supply.

Trauma, steroid use, excessive alcohol, sickle cell disease.

Osteosclerosis

Abnormal increase in bone density and hardening.

Myeloproliferative neoplasms

Systemic mastocytosis

Osteoblastic metastases

Osteosclerotic myeloma (POEM’s syndrome)

Osteomalacia

Softening of bones due to defective mineralization (vitamin D deficiency).

Vitamin D deficiency, poor diet, malabsorption, kidney/liver disease.

Osteopetrosis

Rare genetic disorder causing abnormally dense and brittle bones.

Genetic mutations affecting osteoclast function.

Bony trabeculae are composed of central, mineralized, mature bone and peripheral, newly formed unmineralized bone matrix termed ________

What is the function of bony trabeculae?

What cell type produces osteoid & plays a key role in regulation of HP?

What are Osteocytes, where are they located? What is their origin and physiological role?

●      Osteocytes = osteoblasts (mesenchymal cells) that have been internalized within lacunar spaces of mineralized bone

●      Likely induce osteoclast and osteoblast activity in response to bone injury

●      What are Osteoclasts? Where are they located? What is their origin and physiological role?

●      Children

●      Substantial amounts of unmineralized osteoid in specimens from infants and very young children

Thicker bony trabeculae and greater bone remodeling is normally seen in what gender and age?

●      Adolescent/young adult males - compared with females and older adults

What is osteopenia, when do we call "osteoporosis"?

●      Osteopenia = thinning of bony trabeculae

●      Represents an imbalance of bone homeostasis, with reduced new bone formation

●      Termed osteoporosis → if generalized and associated with reduced bone density testing

●      Osteopenia

What is osteolysis

●      Discrete area of excessive osteoclast-induced bone resorption

●      Thinning of bone here = osteolysis

What is osteonecrosis

●      Nonviable bony trabeculae with loss of osteocytes within lacunar spaces

●      May be associated with necrosis of medullary (HP) cavity

●      Associated with bone marrow infiltration by neoplasms

○      Most common in acute lymphoblastic leukemia


●      Central core of necrotic bone (closed arrows), surrounded by new bone: open arrow

What is osteosclerosis? What is it often associated with?

●      Thickened bony trabeculae that may be anastomosing

●      Radiographically apparent when generalized and prominent

●      Often associated with fibrosis

Osteosclerosis is linked to neoplastic and nonneoplastic disorders of bone and bone marrow
Give 3 neoplastic examples

●      Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) including primary myelofibrosis

●      POEMS

●      Systemic mastocytosis

●      Osteoblastic metastases (prostate and breast carcinoma)

What bone changes may be seen in renal osteodystrophy

●      Variable features of bony trabeculae and BM stroma during course of chronic renal disease

●      Spectrum of sequelae from low and high bone turnover

●      Bone erosion, bone formation, and quiescent phases

●      May see bony trabecular changes linked to secondary hyperparathyroidism

●      May see changes linked to osteomalacia with defective mineralization

●      May see bone islands within medullary space

●      Increased osteoclastic activity in renal osteodystrophy

●      Simultaneous thinning and thickening of bone in renal osteodystrophy

 

What is the pathogenesis of myeloma-associated bony abnormalities

●      Complex pathogenesis via interactions of myeloma cells with BM cells

●      Myeloma cells affect mesenchymal stem cells and other BM stromal cells

○      Suppressed osteoblastogenesis → due to inhibitors secreted by myeloma cells

○      Increased osteoclastogenesis → due to osteoblast deactivation and production of osteoclast-activating factors

○      Osteoclasts produce factors that stimulate myeloma cells

What is osteomalacia? 

●      Excessive osteoid formation with defective mineralization

●      Linked to selected renal disorders

●      Constitutional and acquired types



What changes are seen with Paget disease of the bone?

●      Increased osteoclastic and osteoblastic activity

○      Disorganized woven bone

●      May be familial

Photo: see the disordered whorls

 

What is osteopetrosis - What are the typical changes  

Osteopetrosis: Key Features

Feature

Details

Definition

A genetic disorder characterized by defective osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, leading to excessively dense but brittle bones.

Cause

Mutations in genes regulating osteoclast function (e.g., TCIRG1, CLCN7, RANK, OSTM1).

Bone Changes

- Increased bone density (osteosclerosis) due to defective resorption.
- Thickened, confluent trabeculae.
- Dramatically reduced hematopoietic (HP) space, leading to bone marrow failure.

Clinical Features

- Fracture-prone bones (despite increased density).
- Pancytopenia (due to marrow space obliteration).
- Hepatosplenomegaly (extramedullary hematopoiesis).
- Cranial nerve compression (blindness, deafness, facial palsy).
- Failure of tooth eruption and facial deformities.

Types

- Autosomal recessive ("infantile malignant"): Severe, early-onset, marrow failure.
- Autosomal dominant ("adult benign"): Milder, fractures, no marrow failure.

Treatment

- Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) (for severe forms).
- Interferon-γ, calcitriol (to stimulate osteoclasts).
- Supportive care (fracture management, transfusions for marrow failure).

 

Bone Homeostasis is controlled by complex mechanisms - What are the cellular and non-cellular factors necessary for healthy bone homeostasis?

●      Cellular:

○      Normal numbers & function of osteoblasts, osteoclasts, osteocytes, vasculature, stem cells

●      Non-cellular:

○      Adequate calcium phosphorus, vitamin D, and regulatory factors required (stem cell factor, growth factors, IL-3,4,5,6)

What age-related factor is linked to osteocyte apoptosis and loss of regulation of bone remodeling by osteocytes

●      Estrogen deficiency in women is linked to osteocyte apoptosis and loss of regulation of bone remodeling by osteocytes

Osteopenia/osteoporosis is very common in what gender and age group 

●      Elderly, especially postmenopausal women

Rare constitutional disorders, such as osteopetrosis and some types of osteomalacia, generally manifest in what age group

●      During infancy and early childhood - Severe HP compromise is characteristic

What features should you be looking for when you assess the trabecular bone in a BM trephine biopsy   

●      1) Assessment of adequacy

○      Must be at least 1 cm in length

○      Must show intact, not crushed, bony trabeculae and medullary cavity

●      2) Assessment of bony trabeculae

○      Assess thickness, uniformity, and contours of bony trabeculae

○      Assess for relative proportions of osteoid and mineralized bone including osteoid seams and cement lines

○      Assess for thickening and anastomoses of bony trabeculae

○      Assess lacunar spaces for intact, viable osteocytes or empty lacunar spaces in nonviable bony trabeculae

○      Assess for tiny disconnected strands of bony trabeculae (bone islands)

○      Assess for composite/mixed features of thickened and thinned bony trabeculae with bone islands

■      Typical feature of chronic renal disease

■      Bone islands are disconnected thin segments of bony trabeculae within medullary space

○      Assess for evidence of osteosis fibrosa cystica

■      Islands of osteoblasts and stroma within bony trabeculae

○      Assess for osteoblast rimming

■      Number and extent

○      Assess for osteoclasts

■      Number

■      Howship lacunae localization

●      3) Access for associated fibrosis &/or necrosis of medullary cavity

○      Assess for other BM stromal abnormalities

○      Osteopenia common in severely ill patients with gelatinous transformation (serous fat atrophy)

●      4) Assess for common neoplasms linked to pathology of bony trabeculae

○      Carcinoma

○      Myeloma

○      MPN, primary myelofibrosis, and mastocytosis

When you are assessing bony trabeculae, what patient factors do you need to consider

●      Correlate appearance of bony trabeculae with normal features based on age and sex

What underlying disease/cause should you consider if BOTH thickened AND markedly thinned bony trabeculae are present, especially if associated with bone islands

●      Chronic renal disease

What underlying disease/cause should you consider if bony trabeculae are thickened with disorganized swirls of haphazard bone

●      Paget disease

Metastatic Carcinoma and Sarcoma involving the BM

●      Carcinomas of prostate, breast, lung, and gastrointestinal origins

●      Melanoma

●      Rhabdomyosarcoma

Name 4 common non hematologic tumors involving bone marrow in children. Which is most common?    

●      Neuroblastoma (most common)

What is the term for circulating non hematological tumor cells in blood

Name 4 possible PB Morphologic Findings you might see with Metastatic Carcinoma or Sarcoma involving the BM

Which IHC stain supports epithelial origin

What 2 stains could prove useful in separating neuroblastoma from other mimics?

Congenital Neutropenia

Chediak-Hagashi syndrome

 

Q. Inheritance pattern of Chediak-Hagashi syndrome

Autosomal recessive

 

Q. What gene is affected in Chediak-Hagashi syndrome?

·       LYST gene on chromosome 1q42 that encodes a protein involved in intracellular trafficking of proteins

 

Q. Etiology of Chediak-Hagashi syndrome

Abnormalities of lysosome-related organelle morphology and function resulted in a microtubule polymerization defect which leads to a decrease in phagocytosis.

 

Q. Clinical presentations[QZ7] 

·       Partial oculocutaneous albinism

·       Peripheral neuropathy

·       Decrease in phagocytosis → results in recurrent pyogenic infections

·       Pancytopenia

·       HSM, lymphadenopathy

·       Lymphoid transformation of EBV infection

·       HLH in accelerated disease

 

Q. Morphological abnormalities in Chediak-Hagashi syndrome?

·       Abnormal cytoplasmic inclusions involving the white blood cells (neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils and lymphocytes)

·       Variably sized large aggregates of purple/blue/red granules

 

Q. Prognosis of Chediak-Hagashi syndrome?

·       Most patients die by ten years of age

Myelokathexis in WHIM syndrome

See in Ped Congenital

·       Warts, hypogammaglobulinemia, immunodeficiency, and myelokathexis.

·       A cause of neutropenia characterized by mutations in CXCR4 (also in LPL, IgM MGUS)

Severe congenital neutropenia

See in Ped Congenital

Shwachman-Diamond syndrome

See in Ped Congenital

Congenital Neutrophilic Disorders

MYH9-related disorders

Feature

Details

Definition

A group of autosomal dominant disorders caused by mutations in the MYH9 gene, which encodes non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA (NMMHC-IIA), affecting platelets, kidneys, hearing, and leukocytes.

Gene Mutated

MYH9 (22q12.3)

Main Clinical Syndromes

- May-Hegglin anomaly (macrothrombocytopenia, Döhle-like bodies in neutrophils).
- Sebastian syndrome (similar to May-Hegglin).
- Fechtner syndrome (macrothrombocytopenia + nephropathy + deafness + cataracts).
- Epstein syndrome (similar to Fechtner but without Döhle bodies).

Hematologic Features

- Macrothrombocytopenia (large platelets, low platelet count).
- Bleeding tendency (mild to moderate).
- Döhle-like inclusion bodies in neutrophils (pale cytoplasmic inclusions).

Diagnosis

- Peripheral blood smear: Large platelets, Döhle-like bodies.
- Genetic testing for MYH9 mutations.
- Urine protein analysis (for nephropathy).

Treatment

- Supportive care: Platelet transfusion if bleeding.
- Renal monitoring & management (ACE inhibitors for proteinuria).
- Hearing aids if necessary.

Differential Diagnoses

·       Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)

·       Reactive Döhle bodies

·       Other inherited macrothrombocytopenia syndromes

Pelger-Huet anomaly

Feature

Details

Definition

A benign autosomal dominant disorder characterized by hyposegmentation of neutrophils, caused by a mutation in the LBR (Lamin B receptor) gene.

Cause

Mutation in LBR gene affecting nuclear membrane organization.

Morphology

- Bilobed ("pince-nez") or round nucleus in neutrophils.

- Dense chromatin.

Clinical Significance

- Heterozygous form: No clinical consequences; neutrophils function normally.

- Homozygous form (Pelger-Huët anomaly variant): Associated with skeletal abnormalities.

Differentiation from Acquired Forms

- Acquired (pseudo-Pelger-Huët anomaly) occurs in myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), leukemia, infections, or drug reactions.

- True Pelger-Huët anomaly is benign and hereditary.

hereditary PH anomaly

pseudo PH anomaly

Lysosomal storage diseases (see above)

 

Alder-Reilly Anomaly

Feature

Details

Definition

A rare inherited disorder characterized by coarse, dark-staining granules in leukocytes, resembling toxic granulation but present in all granulocytes, caused by a defect in mucopolysaccharide (MPS) metabolism.

Cause

Associated with mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS) (e.g., Hurler, Hunter).

Morphology

- Prominent, large, dark-purple cytoplasmic granules in neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils.
- Granules represent partially degraded mucopolysaccharides accumulating in lysosomes.

Key Differentiation

- Unlike toxic granulation, Alder-Reilly granules are present in all neutrophils and do not accompany infection or inflammation.
- No Döhle bodies or left shift, differentiating it from a true infection response.

Clinical Features

- If associated with MPS, may present with skeletal abnormalities, hepatosplenomegaly, corneal clouding, and intellectual disability.
- If isolated, no clinical consequences.

Diagnosis

- Peripheral blood smear: Large metachromatic granules in all granulocytes.
- Urine glycosaminoglycan (GAG) test: If MPS is suspected.
- Genetic testing for mucopolysaccharidoses if systemic involvement is present.

Treatment

- No treatment needed for isolated Alder-Reilly anomaly.
- For MPS-related cases: Supportive therapy, enzyme replacement therapy (if available).

Chediak-Higashi Syndrome

See above.

 

 

Transplant topics

Cellular basis of hematopoiesis and stem cell transplantation

 

Q: What are the defining characteristics of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs)?
A:

  • Self-renewal capability: Achieved via asymmetric cell division (one daughter remains a stem cell, the other differentiates).
  • Pluripotency: Can differentiate into all blood cell types (erythrocytes, leukocytes, platelets).

 

Q: What is asymmetric cell division?
A:

  • Produces two daughter cells with different fates: one retains stem cell properties, the other differentiates.
  • Contrasts with symmetric division (identical daughter cells).
  • Critical for maintaining the stem cell pool while producing differentiated cells.

 




Q: How abundant are primitive HSCs in BM, and what are their features?
A:

  • Rarity: ~1 in 10⁴–10⁶ BM cells (extremely scarce).
  • Quiescence: Reside in G₀ phase (non-dividing).
  • Resistance: Insensitive to cytokine stimulation.
  • Division outcomes: Self-renewal or differentiation via asymmetric division.

 

What general changes take place as hematopoietic stem cells undergo differentiation?

 

●      Differentiation through progenitor hierarchy

●      Pluripotent - Multipotent - oligopotent - monopotent progenitors

●      Loss of self-renewal capacity

●      Increased restriction in differentiation potential

 

What regulates hematopoietic cell development?

 

●      Signals provided by the BM microenvironment

●      Heterologous cells (mesenchymal, endothelial, neural)

●      Hematopoietic cells

●      Extracellular matrix cells

 



 

What are 3 sources of stem cells for clinical purposes?

 

●      1. Umbilical cord blood

●      2. Mobilized peripheral blood stem cells (apheresis collection following a mobilization phase) - GCSF, Plerixafor, Cyclophosphamide

●      3. Bone marrow stem cells from harvest

Are there any survival differences between using PB and BM as a source of HSPCs in adults? Children?

 

●      Adults - NO

●      Children - ? YES - more studies needed

●      Retrospective study showed poorer outcomes for children with PB grafts

 

What are the differences for the recipient between PB and BM harvest for transplantation in adults vs children?

 

●      PB

○      Minimal short-medium term toxicities

○      More rapid engraftment

○      Lower risk of graft failure (more CD34+ cells)

○      Fewer earlier complications

○      More frequent chronic GVHD (T-cells)

○      Children had poorer outcomes

●      BM

○      More graft failure

○      Lower rates of acute and chronic GVHD

■      May be superior for non-malignant cases due to lower GVHD

○      More RBCs and plasma (requires modification in ABO mismatch transplant)

■      Plasma or RBC reduce!

 

What are the HLAs in MHC I and MHCII?

 

●      MHC I

○      HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C

○      “I” = think HLA plus 1 letter

●      MHC II

○      HLA DR, HLA DQ, HLA DP, HLA DM, HLA DO

○      “II” = think HLA plus 2 letters

 

Note: Major histocompatibility complex (MHC), group of genes that code for proteins found on the surfaces of cells that help the immune system recognize foreign substances. MHC proteins are found in all higher vertebrates. In human beings the complex is also called the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) system

 

What cells have MHC I? MHC II?

 

●      MHC I - all cells

●      MHC II - Antigen presenting cells

 

What type of donor/HLA matching is the #1 choice?

 

●      Complete HLA-matched sibling donor

 

Why is a sibling donor the #1 choice?

 

●      HLA-matched sibling donors create less GVHD

●      Due to higher chance of match at → minor histocompatibility sites

●      Less morbidity and mortality

 

Note: Minor histocompatibility antigen (also known as MiHA) are receptors on the cellular surface of donated organs that are known to give an immunological response in some organ transplants. They cause problems of rejection less frequently than those of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC).

 

Q: What HLA alleles are matched in a 10/10 donor?
A:

  • MHC I: HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C (both alleles for each).
  • MHC II: HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQB1 (both alleles).

 

Note: 2 alleles for each

 

What is a 10/10 HLA match?

 

●      Match for both alleles at HLA- A, B, C

●      HLA DRB1, DQB1

 

If a 10/10 match is not possible, what is acceptable?

 

●      Single mismatch is acceptable

 

Why do unrelated donors have a higher risk of GVHD than related, even if 10/10 match?

 

●      Unrelated donors more likely to be mismatch at minor histocompatibility antigens

●      Therefore increased risk of GVHD, and increased immunosuppression needed

 

What are other types of stem cells that can be used if there is no HLA-matched donor?

 

●      1. Haploidentical donors

●      2. Umbilical cord blood

 

Note: A haploidentical, or half-matched, donor is usually your mom, your dad or your child. Parents are always a half-match for their children. Siblings (brothers or sisters) have a 50% (1 out of 2) chance of being a half-match for each other.

 

What are the advantages of using cord blood for stem cells?

 

●      1. Less stringent matching

○      Fewer T-cells and T-cells are naive

○      Only need 4/6 match for cord blood

●      2. Quicker

○      Useful if urgent SCT needed

 

What are the disadvantages of using cord blood for stem cells?

 

●      1. Slow rate of engraftment

●      2. Prolonged myelosuppression

●      3. Delayed immune reconstitution

●      4. Higher rates of death from infection

 

What can be done to mitigate the risk of cord blood stem cells?

 

●      1. Use 2 cords with an adequate cell dose

●      2. Methods to expand numbers within UCB donation


Q: What regulates HSC homing to BM?
A:

  • CXCL12/CXCR4 axis: Critical for retention/mobilization.
  • Integrins (VLA-4), selectins (PSGL1), and signaling molecules (Gas, Rac1/2).

 

Q: Agents used to mobilize HSCs for apheresis?
A:

  • G-CSF: Reduces CXCL12 (SDF-1) in BM, enhancing HSC release.
  • Plerixafor: Blocks CXCR4/CXCL12 interaction (synergizes with G-CSF).
  • Chemotherapy (e.g., cyclophosphamide): Induces stress-mediated HSC release.

 

What is the mechanism of G-CSF mobilization?

 

●      Reduction of the SDF-1 (CXCL12) transcripts + proteolytic cleavage of the protein

●      Evasion of phagocytosis by increased CD47 expression

 

Mechanism of action of plerixafor? Is it used alone or in combination with G-CSF?

 

●      Plerixafor blocks the chemokine receptor CXCR4 from binding to CXCL12

●      It’s used in combination with G-CSF

 

Note: plerixafor acts as an antagonist (or perhaps more accurately a partial agonist) of the alpha chemokine receptor CXCR4 and an allosteric agonist of CXCR7. The CXCR4 alpha-chemokine receptor and one of its ligands, SDF-1, are important in hematopoietic stem cell homing to the bone marrow and in hematopoietic stem cell quiescence

 

Q: What is the surrogate marker for HSC count?
A:

  • CD34+ cells (≥2 × 10⁶/kg for PB/BM; ≥1.7 × 10⁵/kg for UCB).

 

What are the minimum number of CD34+ cells/kg required for transplantation? In PB, BM, UCB??

 

●      1) PB/BM

○      >2 x 10^6 CD34+ cells /kg (> 2 million/kg)

○      Improved survival in unrelated transplants

○      > 8 x 10^6 PB are associated with increased GVHD (too much of a good thing)

●      2) UCB

○      Minimal dose is >2.5 x 10^7 nucleated cells/kg or >1.7 x 10^5 CD34+ cells/kg (170,000) - (? round to 200, 000 = might be easier number to remember with 2 million for PB/BM)

What is the relationship between the degree of mismatch, and the number of HSCs needed?

 

●      Greater the degree of mismatch, higher the dose needed

 

What are the advantages/ disadvantages of a sibling donor?

 

Advantages of a sibling donor:

·       Better match at HLA and minor histocompatibility loci

o   Reduced chance of GVHD compared to unrelated donor cell sources.

·       Donor cells can potentially be obtained quickly.

·       Potentially, donor can be easily approached again for additional HSPCs to improve graft function or for T-cells for donor lymphocyte infusion to augment alloimmune response against recipient disease cells.

Disadvantages of a sibling donor

·       Potentially less graft-versus-disease immune response

·       I.e. the opposite of the advantage mentioned above (Reduced chance of GVHD compared to unrelated donor cell sources)

 

What are the advantages and disadvantages of an unrelated donor?

 

Advantages of an unrelated donor

·       Increased graft versus disease compared to sibling donor.
Donors available for common haplotypes.

Disadvantages of an unrelated donor

·       Increased graft versus host response compared to sibling donor.

·       Potentially more difficult to obtain additional HSPCs and donor lymphocytes for graft failure, and increased allo-immune response against recipient disease cells.

 

What are the advantages/disadvantages of a Haploidentical donor?

Advantages

1.     Increased Donor Availability

2.     Faster Transplant Process

3.     Graft-versus-Leukemia (GVL) Effect

·       A stronger immune response against cancer cells, reducing relapse risk.

·       Beneficial in high-risk leukemia or lymphoma.

4.     Option for Post-Transplant Cyclophosphamide (PTCy)

5.     More Ethnic and Racial Diversity

Disadvantages

1.     Higher Risk of Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD)

2.     Higher Risk of Graft Failure

3.     Slower Immune Reconstitution

4.     Increased Relapse Risk (in some cases)

5.     Requires Specialized Centers


What are the advantages/disadvantages of a cord blood graft?
Advantages
• Donor cells available when other cell sources not available.
• Donor cells quickly available.
Disadvantages
• Longer time to engraftment.
• Longer time for immune reconstitution.

Q: Sites of hematopoiesis during gestation?
A:

  • Yolk sac: Weeks 3–6.
  • Fetal liver: Weeks 6–20.
  • Bone marrow: From week 20 onward.

 

Q: Why are HSCs resistant to chemotherapy?
A:

  • Quiescence: Rarely divide, evading antimetabolites.
  • Efflux pumps: High P-glycoprotein expression expels drugs.

 

Which dye can be used to identify the HSCs in flow cytometry?

 

●      Rhodamine-123 or Hoechst-33342 dyes = The HSC efflux pump excludes certain fluorescent dyes

●      Using these dyes in combination with flow cytometry, it has been possible to identify a population of hematopoietic cells with low dye retention, so-called side population (SP) cells.

●      Although this population is markedly enriched for HSCs, SP cells still represent a heterogeneous mix and are not equivalent to pure HSCs.

Q: How are HSCs identified in flow cytometry?
A:

  • Immunophenotype: CD34+, CD38−, Lin−, CD45RA−, Thy1+.
  • Dye exclusion: Rhodamine-123 or Hoechst-33342 (side population cells).

 

What percentage of BM cells express CD34?

 

●      Early studies to isolate humans HSCs found that approximately 1% of human BM cells express CD34.

 

 

ISHAGE Protocol for CD34 Enumeration

 

What is the name of the guidelines used for stem cell enumeration?

●      International Society of Hematotherapy and Graft Engineering

○      Established stem cell enumeration committee to validate a flow cytometric method to quantitate CD34+ cells in PB and aphaeresis products

What are the two methods for Stem cell enumeration? And how are they done?

●      Four parameter two colour panel had been proposed

○      1) Dual platform initially (still at VGH)

■      Uses two analyzers to calculate number of CD34+ cells in a sample

■      1) CBC analyzer to enumerate WBC

■      2) Flow cytometry analyzer to provide the % of CD34+ events (stem cells)

■      The absolute number of CD34+ events is calculated using the denominator of the WBC from the CBC analyzer

○      2) Single Platform (BCCH)

■      Only the flow cytometer is used to provide the CD34+ count

■      Number of kits available using → fluorospheres/beads

■      A known volume and concentration of beads added to the equal volume of the patients sample

■      By mixing known amount of beads with a blood sample, the absolute count is derived directly from the flow cytometer by measuring the → ratio beads and the CD34+ cells in the sample

What are the criteria for identification of true CD34+ cells?

●      Moderate CD45 antigen characteristic of blast cells (lower level than lymphocytes and monocytes)

●      Moderate to strong intensity of CD34 antigen

●      Low side scatter (SS) pattern and Low to intermediate forward angle light scatter(FS) characteristics of blast cells

○      CD34++, CD45+, mod FS and low SS

 

ISHAGE Guidelines Specimen Requirements

●      Specimen requirements

○      ACD and EDTA anti coagulated samples

○      Storage and transport at RT to avoid hemolysis

○      Analyze ASAP, within 24 hours

■      PMNs begin to die. If wait too long, then there will be an artifactual increase in CD34+ cells (denominator will be smaller)

What is the Analysis Protocol for ISHAGE?

●      Analysis Protocol

○      Three tubes: CD45-FITC/CD34-PE x2 (in duplicate), and CD45-FITC/Isotype-PE

■      Wash-out in between (Normal Saline) to ensure no carryover

○      Collect 75,000 CD45+ events and 100 CD34+

●      Sequential gating technique

○      Plot 1: CD45 vs SS

■      To gate out CD45 negative, and to gate on the lymphocytes

○      Plot 2: CD34 vs SSC staining of CD45+

■      To get only events that are 34+

○      Plot 3: CD45 vs SSC of the CD34+ cells

■      To clean up the CD34+ cells that are truly the blast cells based on the dim45

○      Plot 4: Light scatter (FSC/SSC) of CD34+ events

●      Calculate the CD34+ = P2 and P3 and P4 (as below!)

 

 

●      Note: Plot 5 with P6 is an estimate of the % of CD34+ cells if you did not do the ISHAGE protocol!

●      Also, we do a viability dye (ie. 7-AAD) and only include the viable cells

 

 

How do you calculate the CD34+ cells in the Dual platform method?

 

●      CD34 % x WBC = absolute CD34/volume (cells/uL)
