  • Before Engraftment:
    • RBCs should match the recipient to prevent immune attack.
    • Plasma should match the donor to avoid transfusing harmful antibodies.
  • After Engraftment:
    • Both RBCs and plasma should match the donor as the recipient fully transitions to the donor’s hematopoietic system.

 

3. Key Transfusion Medicine (TM) Considerations in SCT

Pre-Transplant:

  • ABO typing of donor & recipient
  • Antibody screen status (alloimmunization risk)
  • Leukoreduction (reduces HLA-alloimmunization & CMV risk)
  • Gamma irradiation (prevents transfusion-associated GVHD)
  • Inventory management, especially platelets

Peri-Transplant:

  • Updated patient TM file
  • Product compatibility confirmation
  • Engraftment tracking

Post-Transplant:

  • Engraftment monitoring (chimerism, ABO switch)
  • Platelet refractoriness (HLA-matched platelets if needed)
  • Communication with home hospital for transfusion needs

 

4. ABO Mismatch Processing for Different Stem Cell Sources

Stem Cell Source

Major Mismatch

Minor Mismatch

Bidirectional

Bone Marrow (BM)

RBC depletion (remove donor RBCs)

Plasma depletion (remove donor plasma)

Both RBC & plasma depletion

Peripheral Blood (PB)

Typically red cell and plasma depleted at source

Cord Blood (CB)

Red cell & plasma depleted before cryostorage

If not, must be washed post-thaw
  • Red Cell Depletion: Minimal loss of CD34+ stem cells
  • Plasma Depletion: Prevents hemolysis from donor antibodies

 

5. Complications of ABO-Incompatible SCT

Major Mismatch:

  1. Acute Hemolysis (Can occur in both major & minor mismatch)
  2. Delayed Red Cell Engraftment
    • Recipient’s antibodies persist for 3-4 months
    • Chimerism may delay hemolysis resolution
  1. Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA)
    • More likely with A-antigen mismatch
    • Non-myeloablative SCT (8-38%) > Myeloablative (16-29%)
    • Treated with EPO, plasma exchange
  1. Peri-Transplant Transfusion Challenges
    • Need RBCs & plasma compatible with both donor & recipient

Minor Mismatch:

  1. Acute Hemolysis with Stem Cell Infusion
    • Depends on donor plasma volume & antibody titers
  1. Passenger Lymphocyte Syndrome (PLS)
    • Donor lymphocytes produce anti-recipient antibodies
    • Leads to DAT+, intravascular hemolysis
    • Rapid onset, usually resolves in 2 weeks

 

6. Definition of Engraftment

To confirm a successful ABO switch, all of the following must be met:

·       No RBC transfusion in the past 90 days

·       DAT-negative

·       Forward group shows no residual recipient cells

 

Infections (viruses, bacteria & parasites) (2)

Infections relevant to hematology

Viruses

Note: COVID 19 will be covered in coagulation lectures

HIV

What sort of virus is HIV? DNA or RNA? -What viral family? What other virus (that is associated with hematological malignancies), belongs to this family?

●      RNA retrovirus infection

●      Retroviruses contain 2 single strands of RNA

●      Lentivirus family

●      HIV-1: 3rd identified retrovirus (after HTLV-1 and HTLV-2)

●      HIV-2: 4th identified retrovirus

At the time of initial infection, what cell type in mucous membranes or skin, does HIV infect?

●      Virus first infects Langerhans (dendritic) cells in mucous membranes or skin

What steps follow the initial HIV infection of Langerhans (dendritic) cells in mucous membranes or skin

●      Infected cells migrate to lymphoid tissues and infect CD4(+) T cells

●      Virus proliferates in T cells and destroys cells

●      HIV Nef protein regulates modulate surface proteins in infected cells = allows efficient viral replication

●      Burst of viremia within days leads to widespread tissue dissemination; targets lymphoid tissue and central nervous system

●      Symptoms of acute retroviral syndrome

Following initial infection, how is an infected host able to control viral replication  

●      Development of* immune response* by infected individual

○      Specific *CD8(+) T-cell (cytotoxic) responses* control viral replication

○      Decrease in viremia and viral load

●      Impaired cytotoxic T-cell responses occur late in infection

What information is provided by measuring CD4 counts by flow cytometric analysis

●      Marker of immunodeficiency

○      Predicts likelihood of developing AIDS and associated complications

●      Acute retroviral syndrome

○      Decreased CD4(+) and CD8(+) T cells, initially

○      Increased CD8(+) T cells after several weeks, decreases CD4:CD8 ratio

●      Advanced stage (AIDS)

○      CD4(+) T-cell count < 200 cells/mm³ or < 14% of total lymphocytes

What would be the characteristic findings by flow cytometric analysis measuring CD4 counts for acute retroviral syndrome

●      Decreased CD4(+) and CD8(+) T cells, initially

●      Increased CD8(+) T cells after several weeks, decreases CD4:CD8 ratio

What would be the characteristic findings by flow cytometric analysis measuring CD4 counts for Advanced stage HIV infection

●       CD4(+) T-cell count < 200 cells/mm³ or

●      < 14% of total lymphocytes

Excluding molecular testing and flow cytometry, name 1 other laboratory test relevant to hematology (hint TM) that may be abnormal with HIV infection

1.     Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test positivity

a.     Not usually associated with hemolysis

2.     Decreased serum vitamin B12 levels

a.     Not indicative of deficiency

3.     Bone marrow evaluation most informative

a.     If symptomatic patient or CD4 count < 50 cells/mm³

Peripheral Blood findings/manifestations during chronic phase of disease

●      Anemia and lymphopenia most common

●      Neutropenia

○      Effect of antiretroviral or antibiotic therapy

○      Myeloid production failure secondary to infection

●      Additional cytopenias often develop at time of AIDS-defining disease

●      Late stage: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

BM findings in HIV/AIDS - How do the findings differ between early & late disease course? 

●      Frequently hypercellular until late in disease course

○      Usually appears reactive

●      Later in disease course

○      Normocellular or hypocellular

○      Reconstitution of cell lineages after HAART therapy

○      Decreased erythroid lineage

■      Consider parvovirus if giant proerythroblasts present

○      Decreased megakaryocytes

■      Directly infected by HIV

Concurrent disorders that may be seen in the BM during AIDS infection (Hint: 3 hematological, one non-hematological neoplastic disease)

1.     Multicentric Castleman disease

a.     Plasmablasts/immunoblasts immunoreactive for HHV8-latent nuclear antigen

2.     Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, plasmablastic lymphoma

a.     EBV often involved in pathogenesis

b.     Underlying immune dysregulation, cytokines, and other viruses also involved

3.     Classical Hodgkin lymphoma

a.     Bone marrow one of most common extranodal sites of disease

4.     Kaposi sarcoma rare in bone marrow

EBV and CMV: Infectious Mononucleosis Syndromes

Epstein-Barr Virus, Cytomegalovirus

 

EBV & CMV belong to what viral family    

 

●      Herpesvirus

●      Double-stranded enveloped DNA viruses

What cell type does EBV infect

 

●      Infects B cells

How does EBV infect B cells

 

●      EBV infects B cells using receptors = CD21, MHC class II

●      Majority of infected B cells are rapidly cleared from circulation in immunocompetent individuals

●      Elicits T-cell and early natural killer (NK)-cell response

Latent EBV infection occurs in what 2 cell types?

 

●      Latency established in *lymphoid cells or fibroblasts*

●      EBV genome circularizes in nucleus of B lymphocytes and is replicated as episome

●      Memory B cells remain quiescently infected and serves as reservoir for lifelong infection

What cell type does CMV infect - How does this compare with EBV?

 

●      Infects epithelial cells, endothelial cells, neuronal cells, smooth muscle cells, fibroblasts, monocytes, macrophages, and T cells

●      Does not infect B cells

 

What % of clinically apparent IM are EBV vs CMV

 

●      80% cases caused by EBV

●      20% caused by CMV

 

Most common viral opportunistic infection in AIDS?    

 

●      CMV

Is primary or secondary CMV infection more common in stem cell and solid organ transplant patients      

 

●      Secondary/reactivation of virus common in stem cell or solid organ transplant patients

●      Infection occurs 1-3 months after transplant if no prophylaxis, 4-8 months if failed prophylaxis treatment

●      CMV viremia seen in 30% of at-risk pediatric lung transplant patients

Symptoms of EBV IM

 

●      Triad of sore throat, fever, lymphadenopathy

●      Symmetrical, slightly tender lymphadenopathy, especially posterior cervical region in adolescents

●      Hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, rash

●      Malaise, headache, myalgias, chills, nausea

●      Studies suggest incubation period of 30-50 days

Symptoms of CMV IM

 

●      Systemic symptoms (typhoidal)

●      Persistent fever may predominate (average duration ~ 19 days)

●      Pharyngitis and tonsillitis are rare

●      Often mild asymptomatic hepatitis

●      Lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly is uncommon

Is the heterophile antibody (monospot) test positive in both EBV & CMV IM?

 

●      No

●      Positive

○      Majority of EBV-associated IM

○      Sensitivity: 90% in adolescents, 80% in children > 4 years of age

○      EBV-specific serology unnecessary to make diagnosis of IM

○      Occasional patients with lymphoma or hepatitis have false-positive results

●      Negative

○      50% of young children with symptomatic EBV infection

○      CMV-associated IM

 

What are the 3 types of Downey atypical lymphocytes    
Most common Downey type of atypical lymphocyte associated with EBV infection?

 

●      Most common type is Downey type II cells

●      Next most common type is Downey type III cells

●      Frequently, cells intermediate between Downey type II and III cells are seen

●      Downey type I cells are most common in young children with EBV and other reactive causes

Autoimmune hemolytic anemia associated with EBV infection due to abs with what antigen specificity?

 

●      Primarily anti-i

Epstein-Barr Virus-Associated Peripheral Blood Findings

 

●      Mild to moderate leukocytosis (10-20 x 10⁹/L)

●      Lymphocytosis

○      1 week after initiation of symptoms

○      Persists up to 8 weeks

●      Atypical lymphocytes with marked heterogeneity

○      Most common type is Downey type II cells

●      Mild thrombocytopenia (< 150 x 10⁹/L) common

●      Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

○      Autoantibodies present (primarily anti-i)

○      Spherocytes and polychromasia

●      Red blood cell clumping

○      Cold agglutinin

What is the only viral infection with specific diagnostic findings in the PB

 

●      Cytomegalovirus

Cytomegalovirus-Associated Peripheral Blood Findings

 

●      Circulating infected endothelial cells typically at feather edge

●      Exclusively seen in immunocompromised patients

●      Characteristic viral inclusions not evident on Wright or Giemsa stained smears

●      Relative lymphocytosis

○      > 10% reactive lymphocytes per 100 white blood cells

○      Increased large granular lymphocytes (T and NK cells)

○      May be indistinguishable from EBV infection, but classic Downey type II cells are infrequent

●      Thrombocytopenia &/or hemolytic anemia

○      Mainly seen in children with congenital CMV infection

 

 



What Epstein-Barr Virus and Cytomegalovirus Bone Marrow Findings may be mistaken for lymphoma?       

 

●      Scattered immunoblasts

○      More common in immunodeficient individuals

○      Cells may resemble Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells

○      May also see Subtle non-necrotizing granulomas, infrequent histiocytosis

○      Rarely fibrin ring granulomas

●     

 

Parvovirus B19 (B19V) infection

 

2 synonyms for Parvovirus B19 (B19V) infection

 

●      Erythema infectiosum

●      Fifth disease

Parvovirus B19 (B19V) propagates efficiently only in what type of cell

 

●      Human erythroid progenitor cells

●      Virus is cytotoxic to cells

●      At least 4 different parvoviruses infect humans

●      Parvoviridae family; genus Erythrovirus

●      B19V is best characterized member of this family

How does B19V gain entry to cells during infection?

 

●      Virus binds blood group P antigen (globoside, Gb4)

P antigen receptors are present on what 3 cell types? 

 

●      Erythroid precursors, megakaryocytes, endothelial cells

In a healthy individual, what is the expected temporal pattern/effect on RBC production by parvo infection     

 

●      Transient aplastic crisis

○      Precipitous drop in hemoglobin

○      4-8 day cessation of red cell production

○      Hemoglobin drops ~ 1g/dL in normal individuals

○      Immune response develops against virus

○      Anemia resolves in 10-19 days

●      Chronic infection with persistent anemia occurs in immunocompromised individuals

○      Primary infection, reinfection or reactivation

 

Parvovirus presentation in healthy individuals

 

●      Self limiting disease in healthy individuals

●      Subclinical erythroid aplasia followed by rash or arthralgias

 

Microscopic Parvovirus infection in the BM

 

●      Minimal erythroid maturation beyond proerythroblast stage unless immunosuppressed

●      IHC for CD71, E-Cadherin

●      Giant proerythroblasts or "lantern cells" are hallmark of infection

 

 

 

●      Bone Marrow

○      Giant proerythroblasts are hallmark of B19V infection

■      Also referred to as "lantern cells"

○      Nuclei have fine megaloblastoid chromatin

○      Nuclear viral inclusions

○      Dark blue, often vacuolated cytoplasm in earliest cells

○      Become larger in size, lose cytoplasmic basophilia, and develop pseudopodia over time

○      Broad-based or "dog ear" cytoplasmic projections

 


What patients are at increased risk of Transient aplastic crisis in PB19 infection?   

 

●      Patients with hemolytic disorders (membranopathy, enzymopathy, hemoglobinopathy)

○      Hereditary spherocytosis

○      Thalassemia, sickle cell disease

○      Red cell enzyme deficiencies

○      Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

●      Patients with concurrent erythroid "stress”

○      Hemorrhage, iron deficiency anemia

○      Malaria, hookworm or other infections

●      Renal or stem cell transplant patients

 

Fetal infection - Highest risk time? Complications?

 

●      Highest risk in 11th-20th week gestation

●      Nonimmune hydrops fetalis

●      Rare abortions, average ~ 9% among infected women

Treatment for Parvo

●      Immunocompetent patients with transient aplastic crisis

○      Red blood cell transfusions

○      Supportive therapy

●      Immunosuppressed patients with persistent infection

○      Temporary cessation of immunosuppression if feasible

○      Administer intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg)

●      Arthralgias and arthritis

○      Respond to nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs

●      Maternal B19V infection

○      Intrauterine blood transfusions

○      Treatment of hydrops fetalis, severe fetal anemia

●      It is spread by daytime-active Aedes mosquitoes, such as A. aegypti and A. albopictus

●      Its name comes from the Zika Forest of Uganda, where the virus was first isolated in 1947

 

Zika Virus Clinical manifestations

 

-        Flu-like illness

-        Fever

-        Conjunctivitis

-        Swelling of hand/feet joints

 

How do you diagnose Zika

 

-        PCR

 

What is the deferral for Zika virus

 

-        21 day waiting period for donating blood after travel from an endemic area

 

Bacteria

Pertussis

  • Etiology/Pathogenesis
    • Infection with Bordetella pertussis, gram-negative, encapsulated, nonmotile, aerobic bacillus, spread by respiratory droplets
  • Clinical Issues
    • Affects ~ 40 million people worldwide with ~ 300,000 deaths annually
    • Progresses to violent coughing with inspiratory "whoop"
    • Diagnosis primarily by culture from nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal swab; PCR and serology can be performed but are less reliable
    • Vaccines (DTap, Tdap) for disease prevention
    • Antibiotics shorten duration of illness and decrease transmissibility
  • Microscopic
    • Necrotizing bronchiolitis, intraalveolar hemorrhage, and fibrinous edema
    • Respiratory epithelium is coated with bacteria; may be denuded with secondary infection, neutrophils within walls of trachea/bronchi are seen
    • Bronchopneumonia with extension into alveolar spaces with secondary infection
    • Interstitial pneumonia or bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia as complications of progressive disease; diffuse alveolar damage in some fatal infections
    • Gram-negative bacilli seen with silver and Giemsa stains
  • Top Differential Diagnoses
    • Adenovirus and other viral infections: Viral cytopathic effect present; special stains negative for bacteria
    • Diphtheria: Respiratory tract pseudomembranes with Gram positive bacilli on surface
    • Mycoplasma pneumonia: Nonspecific lymphocytic/neutrophilic bronchiolitis; special stains negative for bacteria

 

Microscopic features of Pertussis in the blood

●      Leukocytosis with lymphocytosis during early respiratory symptoms

●      WBC count may be > 50 x 10⁹/L for infants

●      Mature-appearing lymphocytes (primarily helper T cells)

●      Condensed chromatin and scant cytoplasm

●      Many cleaved or convoluted nuclei

Tuberculosis

  • Terminology
    • Tuberculosis (TB): Lung infection caused by inhalation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis
  • Clinical Issues
    • Primary infection usually asymptomatic and leads to formation of Ghon complex (apical nodule with calcification) and hilar lymphadenopathy
    • Progressive primary TB occurs when primary foci do not involute and progress to disseminated, cavitary lesions
    • Most common mechanism of secondary TB is reactivation of latent focus of infection
    • Often associated with chronic, debilitating diseases or immunosuppressive states (AIDS, transplant, cancer, diabetes, alcoholism)
    • ~ 1/3 of world's population is infected with TB; more prevalent in underdeveloped countries
    • ~ 10% of HIV-infected patients develop active disease annually
  • Microscopic
    • Basic pathologic manifestation of TB is granulomatous inflammation with necrotizing, palisading, epithelioid granulomas
    • Palisading granulomas can progress to complete fibrosis and calcification
    • Necrotizing granulomas may enlarge to form cavities with central liquefaction that may range from 3-10 cm in diameter
    • Mycobacteria are slender rods measuring 4 μm in length; they cannot be visualized on routine histology and require special stains
  • Ancillary Tests
    • Best stain for M. tuberculosis is Ziehl-Neelsen, which stains acid-fast bacilli
    • Mycobacterial DNA can be demonstrated by PCR

Typical histologic appearance of pulmonary tuberculosis with a necrotizing (caseating) granuloma shows peripheral palisading of histiocytes surrounding a necrotic center (white open arrow).

 

Microscopic features of Tuberculosis in BM

●      Discrete granulomas with epithelioid histiocytes, ± Langhans giant cells, scattered lymphocytes, ± caseation, neutrophils if immunocompromised (granulomas may be absent if immunocompromised)

●      Erythroid hypoplasia ± patchy-type necrosis

●      Detection of acid-fast organisms with ZN stain

Epithelioid cells with cuffing of lymphocytes

Many acid fast bacilli with slender forms are noted in the acid fast stain confirmatory of tubercular etiology

 

 

Anaplasma and Ehrlichia

 

What kind of organism is Ehrlichia?

 

●      Ehrlichiosis is the general name used to describe diseases caused by the bacteria Ehrlichia chaffeensis, E. ewingii, or E. muris eauclairensis

 

What kind of organism is Anaplasma?

 

●      Anaplasma is a genus of bacteria of the alphaproteobacterial order Rickettsiales

●      Anaplasma species reside in host blood cells and lead to the disease anaplasmosis.

●      The disease most commonly occurs in areas where competent tick vectors are indigenous, including tropical and semitropical areas of the world for intraerythrocytic Anaplasma spp.

 

What is the arthropod vector for Anaplasma and Ehrlichia?

 

●      Ticks

●      Ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis are similar tick-borne illnesses that cause flu-like symptoms, including fever, muscle aches and headache. Signs and symptoms of ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis usually appear within 14 days after a tick bite.

 

Which different WCs are infected by Anaplasma and Ehrlichia respectively?

 

●      Ehrlichiosis - Monocytes

●      Anaplasmosis - Neutrophils

 Monocytes from immunocompromised hosts may contain multiple morulae (Wright's stained blood film, patient 9, original magnification × 300).

Severe Anaplasmosis With Multiorgan Involvement in a Rheumatoid Arthritis Patient | Cureus

Rickettsioses, Q-fever

·       (caused by Coxiella burnetii), salmonelloses, borreliosis and brucellosis can be accompanied by a considerable BM lymphocytosis and (fibrin ring-) granulomas

·      Doughnut granulomas are highly evocative of Coxiella infections; however, they are not specific to Coxiella infections and have been seen in CMV, Epstein-Barr virus, Brucella and Salmonella infections, leishmaniasis, Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas, and immune disorders.

Lipogranulomatous bone marrow reaction in a patient suffering from proven complicated subacute borreliosis with reactive large granular lymphocytosis in the peripheral blood (being the reason to perform biopsy). Inset: CD68 staining of a small lipogranuloma in the same patient.

 

Borrelia

 

●      Borrelia is a genus of bacteria of the spirochete phylum

●      It causes Lyme disease, also called Lyme borreliosis, a zoonotic, vector-borne disease transmitted primarily by ticks and by lice, depending on the species of bacteria

●      Direct tests include culture of Borrelia from skin, blood, or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and detection of genetic material by polymerase chain reaction in skin, blood, or synovial fluid

●      Serological and immunological tests too - eg ELISA

 

 

Brucellosis

·       Can cause marrow granulomas, hemophagocytosis, and a peripheral pancytopenia

Trephine biopsy specimen of bone with normocellular bone marrow and a solitary epithelioid granuloma (hematoxylin and eosin stain, original magnification, × 150).

 

Tropheryma whippelli Whipple’s disease

·       PAS-positive organisms are seen within marrow macrophages

·       Confirmation can be accomplished by PCR or EM

Whipple disease involving the bone marrow. Note diastase-resistant PAS+ (foamy) interstitial histiocytes. Inset: presence of analogous histiocytes in a retroperitoneal lymph node of the same patient.

 

Salmonella typhi

·       Associated with pancytopenia due to hemophagocytosis, granulomas, ring granulomas, or bone marrow necrosis

 

Nocardia

  • Etiology/Pathogenesis
    • Infection with Nocardia species, gram-variable, weakly acid-fast bacteria present in soil, standing water, and decaying plants, transmitted by dust inhalation or skin/wound inoculation
  • Clinical Issues
    • Pulmonary, skin (primary or secondary), disseminated, and neurologic disease
    • Majority of cases are in immunosuppressed hosts
    • High mortality with neurologic involvement
  • Imaging
    • Lungs with infiltrates with central necrosis (cavitation)
    • Brain with abscesses or subtle meningitis
  • Microbiology
    • Grow as strict aerobes on wide range of media and temperatures (3 days to several weeks)
    • MALDI-TOF and 16S rRNA sequencing faster and more reliable than phenotypic testing for speciation
  • Microscopic
    • Necrotic abscess with neutrophils, neutrophil debris, and liquefactive necrosis
    • Organisms subtle on H&E; lesions may be paucibacillary
    • GMS: Thin, branching filamentous bacilli (~ 1-μm diameter and up to 20 μm long)
    • Gram variable, mAFB positive with beaded staining pattern
    • Negative on routine AFB stains
  • Top Differential Diagnoses
    • Actinomycosis: Filamentous bacilli negative on mAFB stains
    • Mycobacteria infections: Shorter bacilli strongly positive on routine and modified AFB stains
    • Candidiasis: Thin hyphal forms of wider than Nocardia and mAFB negative

Nocardia stains very well with methenamine silver staining, making this an ideal stain to screen for bacteria in tissue samples. Nocardia filamentous bacilli are easily distinguished from fungal hyphae due to their significantly smaller size (~ 1-μm diameter).

 

Fungal

 

Aspergillus

  • Etiology/Pathogenesis
    • Infection with Aspergillus spp., ubiquitous environment fungi, primarily via inhalation of airborne conidia
    • Most common species of clinical significance includes A. fumigatus, A. flavus, A. niger, and A. terreus
  • Clinical Issues
    • Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), chronic pulmonary aspergillosis, invasive (systemic/disseminated) aspergillosis, rhinosinusitis, endocarditis, and central nervous system involvement
    • Serum positive for galactomannan and (1,3)-β-D-glucan
  • Imaging
    • Chest CT: Halo sign (ground-glass opacity surrounding nodule); air crescent sign (vascular invasion and hemorrhage)
  • Microscopic
    • Regular septate hyaline (nonpigmented) hyphae (3-6 μm in diameter) with dichotomous 45° angle branching; highlighted by GMS and PAS-D stains
    • Angioinvasion is commonly present in invasive disease; tends to grow radially from hematogenous lesions in tissue
    • Neutrophilic inflammation is often present in invasive disease; lesions may show little inflammatory reaction in neutropenic patients
  • Top Differential Diagnoses
    • Candidiasis: Gram-positive yeast, pseudohyphae, and occasional hyphae; positive serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan; negative galactomannan
    • Mucormycosis: Broad, paucisepate, ribbon-like hyphae; negative serum galactomannan and (1,3)-β-D-glucan
    • Hyalohyphomycosis (e.g., fusariosis, scedosporiosis): Hyphae appear similar (lack fruiting bodies); negative serum galactomannan; typically requires culture/PCR to distinguish
    • Concurrent infections with other fungi, including Mucor spp., Candida spp., etc., require molecular/culture, serologic, and histologic correlation

 This PAS-D-stained bronchoalveolar lavage (cell block preparation) shows narrow hyphae with acute-angle branching and septations, consistent with Aspergillus spp.

Mucormycosis

  • Etiology/Pathogenesis
    • Infection with Mucorales, ubiquitous environmental fungi associated with decaying organic matter, via inhalation of spores or though damaged skin
  • Clinical Issues
    • Most cases have rapid course; disseminated infection carries poor prognosis
    • Risk factors include immunosuppression, diabetes mellitus, injection drug use, trauma, burns, malnutrition, iron overload, treatment with deferoxamine
    • Most frequent primary clinical manifestations include rhinocerebral, pulmonary, and cutaneous infections
    • Serum galactomannan and 1,3-β-D-glucan are typically negative
  • Microscopic
    • Nonpigmented, wide (5- to 20-µm), thin-walled, ribbon-like hyphae with few septations and right-angle branching; highlighted by GMS and PAS-D stains
    • Fragmentation and degeneration of fungal elements can make it hard to assess septation and branching
    • Hyphae are angioinvasive, causing tissue necrosis, hemorrhage, and blood vessel thrombosis, particularly in immunocompromised hosts
  • Top Differential Diagnoses
    • Aspergillosis: Narrow hyphae with septations and acute-angle branching; positive serum galactomannan and 1,3-β-D-glucan
    • Candidiasis: Gram-positive yeast, pseudohyphae, and true hyphae; serum 1,3-β-D-glucan positive, galactomannan negative
    • Hyalohyphomycosis (e.g., Fusarium and Scedosporium spp.): narrow hyphae with abundant septations; often positive for 1,3-β-D-glucan, galactomannan negative
    • Concurrent infections with other fungi: Confirmation by cultures, molecular testing, IHC/ISH

 PAS-D staining of a pulmonary artery mass highlights broad, pauciseptate hyphae with 90° angle branching, identified as R. arrhizus by sequencing.

Superficial Mycoses

  • Etiology/Pathogenesis
    • Cutaneous fungal infections limited to stratum corneum, hair, and nails, causing minimal inflammation
  • Clinical Issues
    • Tinea versicolor (Malassezia spp.): Hypochromic or hyperchromic macules with irregular borders that coalesce into patches with fine scale
    • Tinea nigra (Hortaea werneckii): Chronic, hyperpigmented irregular patches
    • Black piedra (Piedraia hortae): Brown or black, fusiform, hard concretions on hair shafts
    • Direct examination with 10-20% potassium hydroxide (KOH) solution and Parker blue ink of skin scrapings or infected hairs
  • Microscopic
    • Tinea versicolor: Basophilic, round yeast and thin, septate hyphae in stratum corneum with spaghetti and meatballs appearance; typically no inflammation present
    • Tinea nigra: Brown pigmented hyphae and blastoconidia in stratum corneum; typically no inflammation present
    • Black piedra: Pseudoparenchymatous mass composed of thick-walled septate hyphae, mimicking arthroconidia, oriented perpendicular to long axis of hair shaft
    • Fungal elements typically visible on H&E-stained sections (can be highlighted by PAS-D)
  • Top Differential Diagnoses
    • Dermatophytosis (tinea): In contrast to Malassezia spp., dermatophytes appear transparent and are difficult to detect on H&E-stained sections and frequently elicit neutrophilic and eosinophilic inflammation
    • Pediculosis capitis: Concretions on hair shaft due to nits and lice; lack fungal elements
    • Melanocytic nevus or melanoma: Neoplasm composed of nevomelanocytes; lack pigmented yeast and hyphae in stratum corneum

 Numerous, somewhat basophilic, thin septate hyphae (black open arrow) and blastoconidia (black solid arrow) are readily evident in the stratum corneum on routine H&E-stained sections with an appearance that has been likened to spaghetti and meatballs.

Blastomycosis

  • Etiology/Pathogenesis
    • Infection via inhalation of Blastomyces spp. fungal conidia
    • Predominantly Blastomyces dermatitidis; other spp. include Blastomyces gilchristii, Blastomyces helicus, Blastomyces percursus, and Blastomyces emzantsi
    • Endemic areas in North America: Southeastern USA, Mississippi and Ohio River Valleys, USA and Canadian provinces around Great Lakes and St. Lawrence River
  • Clinical Issues
    • Most common sites: Pulmonary, cutaneous, osseous
    • No clinical or radiographic features are specific, and spectrum of disease overlaps with those of other fungal pathogens, mycobacteria, and malignancy
    • Immunocompromised patients have more aggressive clinical course
    • Visualization of characteristic yeast forms or growth of fungus in culture is necessary for definitive diagnosis
  • Microscopic
    • Spherical multinucleated yeast cells (8-15 μm) with single broad-based budding, thick refractile wall
    • Pyogranulomatous inflammation
  • Ancillary Tests
    • Positive for GMS, PAS-D, Congo red stains
    • Variable for Fontana-Masson stain
    • Negative for Gram stain
  • Top Differential Diagnoses
    • Histoplasmosis: Small yeast with narrow-based budding
    • Candidiasis: Gram-positive yeast, pseudohyphae, lack of broad-based budding
    • Cryptococcosis: Variably sized yeast with narrow-based budding and mucicarmine-positive capsule
    • Paracoccidioidosis: Yeast with multiple points of budding
    • Coccidioidomycosis: Large spherules with endospores, no budding

 High magnification of a skin section on an H&E stain shows multiple multinucleate Blastomyces yeast cells. Thick cell wall as well as broad-based budding at early (black solid arrow) and late (black open arrow) stages are seen.

Candidiasis

  • Etiology/Pathogenesis
    • Commensal organisms associated with skin and gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts of humans
    • > 20 different species associated with disease, including Candida albicans, Nakaseomyces glabratus (previously C. glabrata), C. parapsilosis, C. tropicalis, Pichia kudriavzevii (previously C. krusei), C. dubliniensis, and C. auris
    • Yeast form associated with dissemination; hyphal form associated with adhesion and tissue invasion
  • Clinical Issues
    • Diseases range from superficial, invasive, to disseminated infections, depending on host immune status
    • Treated with amphotericin B, azoles, and echinocandins
    • (1,3)-β-D-glucan elevated in candidemia/dissemination
    • Most species grow within 3-5 days; MALDI-TOF MS increasingly used for identification
  • Microscopic
    • Gram-positive yeast (2-6 μm in diameter), pseudohyphae, and septate hyphae highlighted by PAS-D and GMS stains
    • Suppurative inflammation and necrosis is often seen, but inflammation can be minimal; giant cells and granulomas are sparse
  • Top Differential Diagnoses
    • Aspergillosis: Septate hyphae; positive galactomannan
    • Trichosporonosis: Yeast-like cells (3-8 µm), pseudohyphae, hyphae with arthroconidia
    • Histoplasmosis: Frequently intracellular yeast (2-4 µm), narrow-based budding, granulomatous inflammation
    • Cryptococcosis: Yeast (4-10 µm), narrow-based budding, Fontana-Masson and mucicarmine positive
    • Sporotrichosis: Yeast (2-6 µm), narrow-based or tube-like budding; Splendore-Hoeppli phenomena common
    • Saccharomyces spp. infection: Gram-positive budding yeast, short pseudohyphae

 GMS staining highlights small to medium-sized yeast and pseudopyphae of C. dubliniensis.

Coccidioidomycosis

  • Etiology/Pathogenesis
    • Caused by dimorphic fungi, Coccidioides immitis and Coccidioides posadasii
    • Found in soil in southwestern USA and parts of Mexico and Central and South America
    • At body temperature, spores develop into endospore-containing spherules, which enlarge and rupture
  • Clinical Issues
    • Incidence (USA): 8,232-22,634 reported cases/year
    • Primary pulmonary disease is often self-limiting
    • Symptomatic persons present after 1-3 weeks with fatigue, cough, dyspnea, headache, night sweats, myalgias, and rash
    • Disseminated disease is rare, affecting musculoskeletal, soft tissues, and meninges in immunocompromised
    • Treated with oral azoles or amphotericin B
  • Microbiology
    • Hyphae are thin and septate with 5- to 8-μm arthroconidia
    • High risk for inhalation exposure for laboratory personnel
  • Microscopic
    • Necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with large, thick-walled spherules (100 μm, containing endospores up to 5 μm)
    • Surrounding infiltrate is often rich in chronic inflammatory cells, eosinophils, neutrophils, and giant cell reactions
    • Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and granulomatous dermal inflammation are common in cutaneous disease
    • GMS stains highlight spherules, endospores, and hyphae (if present)
    • Endospores are PAS positive, but larger/mature spherules are negative
  • Top Differential Diagnoses
    • Rhinosporidiosis and adiaspiromycosis: Larger spherules
    • Histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, and blastomycosis: Overlap in size with endospores but exhibit budding yeast

 Skin biopsy of coccidioidomycosis demonstrates several large spherules (black open arrow) containing numerous small endospores amidst acute and chronic inflammation. (From DP: Nonneoplastic Derm.)

Cryptococcosis

  • Etiology/Pathogenesis
    • Infection with Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii via inhalation of spores
  • Clinical Issues
    • Most cases are seen in immunocompromised patients: HIV infection, prolonged use of glucocorticoids or immunosuppressants, history of stem cell and organ transplants, malignancies
    • Lung (primary) and central nervous system and skin (secondary) are most common sites of infection
    • Untreated disseminated Cryptococcus infection has mortality rate of up to 100%
    • Cryptococcal antigen (CRAG) testing (CSF, serum) have false-positives due to Trichosporon spp.
  • Microbiology
    • Culture differentiates between C. neoformans and C. gattii (usually 3-5 days to grow)
  • Microscopic
    • Encapsulated, spherical to oval yeast cells (5-10 μm in diameter) with narrow-based budding and polysaccharide capsule
    • Yeast cells are positive for GMS, PAS, Fontana-Masson stains
    • Mucicarmine and Alcian blue stain polysaccharide capsule
    • Granulomatous, mixed suppurative and granulomatous, and minimal/absent inflammatory reactions (immunocompromised) may be observed
  • Top Differential Diagnoses
    • Candidiasis: Gram positive, Fontana-Masson negative, pseudohyphae common
    • Histoplasmosis: Fontana-Masson and mucicarmine negative; more regular in size
    • Blastomycosis: Larger in size (8-15 µm in diameter) with broad-based budding; may be Fontana-Masson positive with weak mucicarmine staining

 Methenamine silver staining highlights numerous yeasts of varying sizes, including many with crushed appearances, and occasional narrow-based budding, features typical of Cryptococcus spp.

Histoplasmosis

  • Etiology/Pathogenesis
    • Infections caused by dimorphic fungi Histoplasma capsulatum or Histoplasma duboisii via inhalation of microconidia
  • Clinical Issues
    • Most prevalent endemic mycosis in USA: Mississippi and Ohio River valleys
    • Most infections in immunocompetent patients are asymptomatic or self-limited
    • Disseminated disease mostly occurs in immunocompromised individuals
    • Enzyme immunoassays are available to detect Histoplasma antigens in urine or serum
  • Microscopic
    • Oval small yeast cells (2-4 μm in diameter) with narrow-based budding
    • Yeasts tend to cluster within macrophages
    • Associated with granulomatous inflammation
    • GMS positive; Gram and melanin stains negative
  • Top Differential Diagnoses
    • Emergomycosis: Similar size with narrow-based budding; distinguish by culture/molecular testing
    • Candidiasis: Similar size, gram positive, pseudohyphae
    • Cryptococcosis: More size variability; Fontana-Masson and mucicarmine positive
    • Coccidioidomycosis (endospores): Similar size, no budding
    • Blastomycosis: Large with broad-based budding; distinguish from by H. duboisii culture/molecular testing
    • Pneumocystosis: Cysts lacks budding, focal thickenings in cyst wall
    • Penicilliosis: Yeast-like cells within macrophages, binary fission with central septum
    • Leishmaniasis, toxoplasmosis, Chagas disease: No budding, negative GMS/PAS-D

 Note the variable morphology displayed by Histoplasma yeast forms with narrow-based budding (white open arrow) and variability in yeast size.

Pneumocystosis

  • Etiology/Pathogenesis
    • Pneumocystis jiroveci is ubiquitous parasitic ascomycetous fungus causing opportunistic disease [i.e., Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP)] associated with HIV infection, immunodeficiencies, and malnourishment
    • Asexual trophic (1- to 4-µm) and sexually reproductive cystic (3- to 5-µm) forms
  • Clinical Issues
    • Presents with dyspnea, dry cough, fever, usually of > 4 weeks duration
    • High mortality rate (20-80%) regardless of HIV status
    • Immunofluorescence (gold standard), quantitative real-time PCR, serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan
    • Cannot be cultured in vitro; serology not useful
  • Imaging
    • Bat wing appearance on chest x-ray of diffuse bilateral perihilar infiltrates (ground-glass opacities)
  • Microscopic
    • Intraalveolar eosinophilic foamy proteinaceous material forming alveolar casts, variable interstitial plasma cells, reactive pneumocyte hyperplasia; granulomatous inflammation less common
    • GMS stain highlights uniformly sized nonbudding cyst forms (3-5 μm); spherical, boat or crushed ping-pong ball shape with intracystic bodies
  • Top Differential Diagnoses
    • Noninfectious (e.g., pulmonary edema, alveolar lipoproteinosis): Negative IFA or molecular testing, nonresponsive to antimicrobials, often immunocompetent
    • Cryptococcosis: Narrow-based budding yeast forms; Fontana-Masson and mucicarmine (capsule) positive
    • Histoplasmosis: Small yeast with narrow based budding, no internal basophilic dots
    • Tuberculosis: Necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with positive AFB stain or mycobacterial culture

 A bronchial washing with GMS stain demonstrates round (black curved arrow) to boat-shaped cysts (black open arrow) with nuclei adjacent to the cell wall (black solid arrow). (Courtesy R. Brynes, MD, CDC/PHIL.)

Q. Which malarial species have macrocytosis?

 

●      Ovale & Vivax

 

Q. Which malarial species have schuffner dots?

 

●      Ovale & Vivax

●      If see Schuffner dots, call it P. ovale/vivax

●      Schuffner dots are the most reliable morphological findings in Pv and Po.

 

Q. Differences between Ovale and Vivax? And Malariae? And Falciparum

 

Ovale:

-        Enlarged Oval RBC with FIMBRIATED edges

-        6-12 (fewer) merozoites per schizont

-        Merozoites in Rosette configuration (Rosettes kinda look like an “O”!)

-        Coarse Schuffner dots

-        Infects retics

 

Vivax

-        Enlarged Oval RBC WITHOUT fimbriated edges

-        12-24 (more) merozoites per schizont (Very increased in Vivax)

-        Merozoites in RANDOM configuration

-        Fine Schuffner dots

-        Infects retics

 

Malariae

-        Round RBC no fimbria, not enlarged

-        6-12 (fewer) merozoites per schizont

-        Merozoites may be in rosette configuration

-        No Schuffner dots

-        Infects mature RBC

-        THICK bands!

-        THICK rings

 

Falciparum

-        Normal RBC size

-        No Schizont

-        No Schuffner dots

-        Fine rings

-        Multiple rings per

-        Accole forms

-        Banana Gametocytes*

Name 4 malaria species, mention identifying morphologic features for each one of them which helps with differentiation, give two non-morphologic tests for speciation

 

Part 1: morphologic features

 

●      Macrocytic

o       Vivax:  RBC are enlarged, all stages of life cycle present, sometimes multiple parasites per cell [P. VIVAX TROPHOZOITES HAVE MORE PROMINENT AMEBOID FEATURES]

o       Ovale: RBC are enlarged, RBC are fimbriated, all stages but less so than than vivax, low parasitemia [P. OVALE SCHUFFNER DOTS COARSER, MORE NUMBEROUS, AND APPEAR EARLIER IN RING STAGE]

●      Normocytic

o       Falciparum: RBC are normal size, often multiple ring forms, usually only ring forms are seen, rings are smaller and delicate with “double dots” like a pair of headphones, aplicae forms, high parasitemia, crescent shaped gametocyte (“banana” shape) [DOUBLE CHROMATIN DOT RINGS ARE COMMON, MAURER DOTS BECOME RECOGNIZABLE IN TROPHOZOITES]

o       Malariae: RBC are normal size, No RBC changes, lowest parasitemia, all stages present [PRESENCE OF BAND FORM TROPHOITES]

●      Detection and identification of malarial parasites is facilitated if blood films are stained with a Giemsa stain at pH 7.2 (normal Wright Giemsa or MGG blood films are stained at pH of 6.8). Leishman stain may also be used (VGH)

o       At this pH P. vivax and P. ovale have different tinctorial qualities from non-parasitized cells

 

Part 2: non morphological tests

 

●      Non-morphological tests include PCR and immunochromatography

●      PCR

o       Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays are the most sensitive and specific method to detect malaria parasites

o       PCR-based assay detect parasite DNA

●      Immunochromatography:

o       Antigen detected = histidine-rich protein 2 (HRP2) is specific for P. falciparum pfLDH

o       Parasite LDH detects pan-malaria infection

o       Plasmodium aldolase (PMA) or parasite lactate dehydrogenase (pLDH)

o       Summary:

▪        3 possible antigens

●      Histidine-rich protein 2 (HRP2)-> P.f

●      Plasmodium aldolase (PMA)

●      Parasite lactate dehydrogenase (pLDH)-> Pan

o       Rheumatoid arthritis patients → may show false positive

o       Note these kits are less sensitive for ovale and malariae species

o       Note the sensitivity is generally 100 parasites per ul compared to expert microscopy 5-10 parasite per ul

 

●      Source: Bain Blood Cells 2nd edition p. 153

●      Source: Dacie and Lewis p.109

 

Note: although microscopy remains the gold standard diagnostic test for malaria in clinical settings, polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based assays can have 100-fold greater sensitivity, especially in the setting of low parasitemia or subclinical infections

 

 

2 stains for thick film?

 

●      Giemsa

●      Leishman

 

Thick film pH?

 

●      7.2 for Malaria to see → Schuffner dots (can use Giemsa or Lieshman stain)

 

What is the benefit of the thick film?

 

●      Higher concentration of parasites = incr. sensitivity

 

4 benefits of using a film vs rapid detection kit?

 

●      Rapid test cannot speciate (thin can)

●      Rapid test cannot quantitate

●      Rapid test will remain prolonged after infection cleared

●      Can miss co-infections

 

What is the method for quantifying malaria?

 

●      Thin film examination

 

Q. PCR for malaria?

 

●      Very sensitive

●      PCR is not quantitative

 

 

What other parasite may mimic malaria on a blood film?

 

●      Babesia

 

 Note: Be able to differentiate Falciparum from Babesia (below - note maltese cross)

 

 

 

·        Babesia ring forms in blood

o            See in 1-20% of RBCs

§            Up to 85% of RBCs in splenectomized individuals

·        Peripheral blood smear

o            Normal to slightly increased WBC count

o            Possible hemolytic anemia

o            Thrombocytopenia

·        Bone marrow

o            Increased erythropoiesis and hemophagocytosis

Two ring forms of Babesia are seen in this erythrocyte (black solid arrow). Rings are oval, round, or pear-shaped, and each has a chromatin dot. Differentiation from Plasmodium falciparum rings is difficult when distinctive features of Babesia are not present.

In high parasitemia, extracellular Babesia merozoites (black solid arrow) are found singly or in syncytial groups. Ring forms of P. falciparum are not observed outside of cells, except adjacent to recently destroyed erythrocytes.

Up to 12 rings (or Babesia merozoites) may be seen per red cell (black curved arrow). The distinctive finding of a Maltese cross, in which 4 merozoites coalesce and form a cross, is rare in Babesia microti infections.

 

 

 

 

Filaria

The Filarioidea are a superfamily of highly specialised parasitic nematodes. Species within this superfamily are known as filarial worms or filariae (singular "filaria"). Infections with parasitic filarial worms cause disease conditions generically known as filariasis.

 

What are the sheathed filaria vs unsheathed?

 

1.     Sheathed:

a.     Wuchereria bancrofti

b.     Loa loa

c.     Brugia malayi

2.     Unsheathed

a.     Mansonella perstans

b.     Mansonella ozzardi

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Leishmania

 

Leishmania is a genus of trypanosomes that are responsible for the disease leishmaniasis.

 

How is Leishmaniasis transmitted

 

-        Sand fly

 

What are the clinical features of Leishmaniasis

 

-        The disease can present in three main ways:

-        Cutaneous, mucocutaneous, or visceral.

-        The cutaneous form presents with skin ulcers

-        The mucocutaneous form presents with ulcers of the skin, mouth, and nose.

-        The visceral form starts with skin ulcers and later presents with fever, low count of red blood cells, and enlarged spleen and liver.

-        Potential cause of massive splenomegaly (Kala-Azar)

 

Blood film findings in leishmaniasis?

 

●      Leishmaniasis is diagnosed in the hematology laboratory by direct visualization of the amastigotes (Leishman–Donovan bodies = specific round forms 2 to 4 mm in diameter - see image below).

 

 

●      Buffy-coat preparations of peripheral blood or aspirates from marrow, spleen, lymph nodes, or skin lesions should be spread on a slide to make a thin smear and stained with Leishman stain or Giemsa stain (pH 7.2) for 20 minutes.

●      Amastigotes are seen within blood and spleen monocytes or, less commonly, in circulating neutrophils and in aspirated tissue macrophages.

●      They are small, round bodies 2–4 μm in diameter with indistinct cytoplasm, a nucleus, and a small, rod-shaped kinetoplast. Occasionally, amastigotes may be seen lying free between cells

 

 

 

 

 

 

Trypanosoma

 

-        Trypanosoma is a genus of kinetoplastids (class Trypanosomatidae), a group of unicellular parasitic flagellate protozoa

-        Corkscrew-like motion

-        The majority of species are transmitted by blood-feeding invertebrates,

-        Tse Tse fly = vector of African trypanosomiasis

-        Know how to distinguish these morphologically

-        Know a bit about Chagas disease

 

 

 

 



 

 

 

 [QZ1]Obliterative phlebitis refers to inflammation and fibrosis of a vein, leading to occlusion (obliteration) of its lumen. It is most commonly observed in certain inflammatory and neoplastic conditions, particularly IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD).

 [QZ2]Chédiak–Higashi syndrome (CHS) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder that arises from a mutation of a lysosomal trafficking regulator protein, which leads to a decrease in phagocytosis. The decrease in phagocytosis results in recurrent pyogenic infections, albinism, and peripheral neuropathy.

 [QZ3]Griscelli syndrome (GS) is a rare autosomal recessive multisystem disorder of pigmentary dilution of skin, silver gray hair, variable immunodeficiency, neurological impairment, and abnormal accumulation of melanosomes in melanocytes.

 [QZ4]Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (HPS) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by oculocutaneous albinism, a bleeding diathesis, and other organ involvement specific to certain types [1-3]. Eleven types of HPS associated with mutations in 11 different genes have been recognized

 [QZ5]Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is a group of rare disorders caused by mutations in different genes involved in the development and function of infection-fighting immune cells. Infants with SCID appear healthy at birth but are highly susceptible to severe infections.

 [QZ6]X-linked lymphoproliferative disease (XLP) is a disorder of the immune system and blood-forming cells that is found almost exclusively in males. More than half of individuals with this disorder experience an exaggerated immune response to the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).
